name: Ajrakh
tagline: Indigo, madder and mud, printed block by block on both sides of the cloth.
facts: Form: block-printed, resist-dyed cotton in indigo and red
Clusters: Ajrakhpur and Dhamadka (Kutch), Barmer (Rajasthan) and Sindh
Kutch Ajrakh has received a GI certificate (reported 2024)
Traditionally worn by Maldhari herders in Kutch
art: Ajrakh is printed on both sides of cloth with carved wooden blocks, using resists and natural dyes. Sources describe indigo for blue, madder or alizarin for red, and iron for black. The Mingei essay lists indigo, madder and iron acetate.

Live History India says the process has up to 14 steps. The cloth is washed, then printed and washed repeatedly. Harda gives a yellow base and helps fix dyes. Lime, alizarin, indigo and camel dung are among the materials. Resist paste protects parts of the cloth from dye. Outlook Traveller says a full piece can take up to three weeks and may be washed up to 20 times.

The patterns are built in repeating grids called jaal, with a central field and borders. Wikipedia names motifs such as Mohar, Ghaleecho, Kakar and Chaanp, and says circles and dots are very common. Live History India lists circles, trefoils and floral motifs. Few traditional blocks survive.
artist: Ajrakh is the work of Khatri families, and Live History India adds the Khoja Sheikhs, who are Muslim converts from the Khatri community. Mingei's essay says oral history brings the Kutch Khatri family from Sindh in the 16th century.
Master printer Sufiyan Khatri is named by Outlook Traveller as having run an ajrakh workshop in Hiroshima, Japan. Other names appear in sources but we have not verified them.
Mingei describes a design education programme running since 2005 for Khatri artisans, with 34 graduates by 2019. Some artisans are growing their own indigo and moving to smaller, unique orders.
place: In Kutch, Dhamadka was the older printing village. Live History India says it was destroyed in the 2001 earthquake, and artisans later founded Ajrakhpur, about 43 km away. Other sources tie the move to water shortage, so reasons differ. Khavda is also named as a Kutch centre.
Printing needs a lot of clean water. Mingei says large workshops use thousands of litres a day, and an effluent treatment system was launched in Ajrakhpur in 2022 so water can be reused for washing.
In Rajasthan, Live History India names Barmer as a third cluster, alongside Sindh. We found no source that explains Barmer's history in detail.

history.what: Some historians link ajrak to the Indus Valley because of cloth patterns on the Mohenjo-daro Priest-King bust. Live History India notes that direct cloth evidence is lacking.
Mingei says indigo trade in western India is documented from at least the 14th century.
Khatri printers are said to have come from Sindh to Kutch. Other sources say about 400 or 500 years ago.
Mingei says mill-made cloth took over many markets, and printers began selling to distant cities.
The earthquake destroys Dhamadka, and Ajrakhpur is founded.
An effluent treatment plant is started at Ajrakhpur.
Outlook Traveller reports that Kutch Ajrakh artisans received a GI certificate.

future: Training: keep block-carving and dyeing taught in the families, with design education for the young.
Livelihood: smaller, direct orders and fair prices for natural-dye work.
Materials: protect water supply and support farm-grown indigo.
Documentation: preserve the old blocks, which few survive.
Protection: the GI should separate hand-printed Kutch Ajrakh from machine-printed copies.

name: Apatani Weaving
tagline: Back-strap loom cloth with straight bands and zig-zags, woven by Apatani women.
facts: Form: hand-woven cotton shawls and jackets
Loom: portable back-strap loom, called Chichin in some sources
Weavers: Apatani women
Used at: Dree and Myoko festivals, weddings and rituals
art: Apatani cloth is woven on a portable back-strap loom made of bamboo and wooden sticks. One end is tied to a fixed object and the other goes around the weaver's waist. She controls the tension of the threads by leaning back or forward. Government-linked handloom listings call this loom the Chichin and say one weaver can set it up and work it alone.

The main pieces are shawls, called jig-jiro or jilan in the sources I read, and jackets called supuntarii. The cotton is grown locally and is called empya. One account lists the tools used before weaving: a tool for ginning, a spindle for spinning and a frame for making yarn loops.
Colours come from forest leaves, roots and bark. One article names tamin as a source of red-orange and sankhii as a source of brown-yellow. Other sources say plant dyes are used but do not list them.

The look is geometric and angular. Straight border bands and zig-zags are common, and one writer says they recall the mountains. Curves are rare, though one source says priests may wear shawls with spiral designs. Government-linked listings say Apatani priests wear a special shawl on ceremonial occasions.
artist: Weaving among the Apatani is done almost entirely by women. Skills pass from mothers to daughters, according to one cultural article. I did not find named master weavers in the sources I could read, so none are named here.
The cloth is worn at Dree, an agricultural festival, and at Myoko, which one source links with friendship and prosperity. It is also used at weddings and rituals.

Sources I read say fewer young people take up weaving as they move to towns for work, and that cheap power-loom copies compete with hand-woven cloth. NGO workshops are mentioned as one response, but I could not check which ones.
place: The Apatani live in the Ziro valley, the headquarters area of Lower Subansiri district in Arunachal Pradesh. Sources describe weaving as part of village life there alongside farming.
Apatani are also known for their bamboo work. Down To Earth says they have managed bamboo plantations for decades. Cloth, bamboo and cane together make up much of the valley's craft.

history.what: Sources I read give no date for when back-strap weaving began among the Apatani. Weaving is described only as a long-standing women's skill passed down in families.
Cloth is tied to Dree and Myoko festivals, weddings and rituals, and to special priestly shawls.
The Gazetteer of Arunachal Pradesh (1980) is cited by a handloom listing for the Tangsa textile; I did not find a dated Apatani source in it.
Drishti IAS reported that a firm had applied for a Geographical Indication (GI) tag for Apatani textile.
A 2023 education article lists Apatani among Arunachal textiles with GI tags, along with Monpa, Nyishi, Adi, Galo and Tai Khamti. Check the official GI registry for dates and registration details.

future: Training: keep mother-to-daughter teaching alive with village workshops in back-strap weaving and natural dyeing.
Livelihood: use the GI listing, where confirmed, to sell cloth under the Apatani name at fair prices.
Materials: protect access to local cotton and to the forest plants used for dye.
Documentation: record dye recipes, tool names and motif meanings with the weavers who know them.
Protection: help weavers tell hand-woven cloth from power-loom copies, for example with labels.

name: Bagh Print
tagline: Red and black hand-block prints made in a small town where the river is part of the dye house.
facts: Place: Bagh, Dhar district
Craft: wood-block printing with natural dyes
Colours: mainly red (alum with tamarind) and black (ferrous sulphate)
GI registered in 2008, per Wikipedia
art: Bagh print is hand block printing on cloth, made in Bagh in Dhar district. Wikipedia describes designs in red and black on a white or off-white ground. They include geometric shapes, paisleys and floral forms such as jasmine and mango. Down To Earth adds that symmetry is the key principle, and the florals look like Rajasthan's Sanganeri prints.

The work is slow and wet. The cloth is first soaked in a mix that includes salt, hot water and goat dung (Down To Earth) or castor oil (Wikipedia), which gives it an off-white base. Red comes from alum with tamarind seed, and black from ferrous sulphate. Blocks are pressed by hand onto cloth laid over padded layers. Down To Earth says the blocks come from Pethapur in Gujarat.

After printing, the cloth rests for some days, then is washed and beaten in the river. It is boiled in an alizarin bath in a step called bhatti, then dried in the sun. Wikipedia says an expert can print about five yards in two to three hours.
artist: Bagh print is tied to Khatri families. Wikipedia names Mohammed Yusuf Khatri, Mohammed Bilal Khatri and Mohammed Kazeem Khatri as key figures, and says Yusuf's bed cover, which used 1,200 blocks, won a National Award in 1984. It also names Ismail Sulemanji Khatri and Abdul Kadar Khatri (1961 to 2019) as master craftspersons.

Where the Khatris came from is not settled. Wikipedia lists possibilities, including settlers from Jawad, printers from Rajasthan, or Khatris who came from Larkana in Sindh about 400 years ago. Down To Earth also says one of the district's oldest artisans migrated from Sindh.
Down To Earth notes that men dominate the industry and that women are largely absent. It also says the craft slows during the monsoon, when many artisans grow maize.
place: Bagh is a town about 100 km from the Dhar district headquarters, near Mandu, according to Down To Earth. The Khatri community chose it mainly for the nearby Baghini river. The river is used to wash and treat cloth, and artisans often say its water helps the dyes. Wikipedia reports this belief as a claim.

The town also has the Bagh Caves, whose paintings Wikipedia says inspired some motifs. The Down To Earth article suggests recycling wastewater and harvesting rainwater, because the craft depends so much on water.

history.what: Wikipedia says the craft is believed to be over 1,000 years old, but its origins are uncertain.
Some Khatri printers are said to have come from Sindh; sources differ, and other origins are also proposed.
Wikipedia says many craftsmen moved to synthetic fabrics, though some kept the craft alive.
Mohammed Yusuf Khatri's bed cover wins a National Award (Wikipedia).
The Khatri family develops designs for urban tastes and new uses of block printing (Wikipedia).
Bagh print is registered as a Geographical Indication; its logo was approved in 2015 (Wikipedia).

future: Training: Down To Earth reports that self-help group training has helped new printers.
Livelihood: women are largely absent; the article suggests women's groups for block carving.
Materials: blocks are brought from Gujarat; local carving would keep more income in Bagh. Natural dyes are the craft's selling point, but some artisans now use faster synthetic colours.
Documentation: record the families, patterns and block sets before they are lost or copied.
Protection: use the GI mark and water-saving methods so the craft can keep using the Baghini.

name: Bagru and Sanganer Block Printing
tagline: Mud-resist indigo in Bagru, fine flowers on white in Sanganer: two printing towns near Jaipur.
facts: Craft community: Chhipa (Chippa) printers
Bagru: dabu mud-resist and natural dyes
Sanganer: fine floral prints on white
Both carry Geographical Indication tags (Sanganer 2010; Bagru 2024)
art: Bagru and Sanganer are two towns near Jaipur known for hand block printing on cloth. The prints are made with carved wooden blocks dipped in dye and pressed by hand onto stretched fabric.

Bagru prints use natural dyes. Wikipedia lists indigo for blue, madder root for red and iron filings for black. The special Bagru technique is dabu, a mud resist: a paste of clay, gum and millet chaff is printed on the cloth so that dye cannot reach those parts. Blocks are carved from hardwoods such as sheesham or teak. The designs are often floral, geometric or drawn from nature, in earthy tones.

Sanganeri printing is finer. Incredible India says artisans carve designs into seasoned teak blocks, dip them in natural dyes and press them on cloth, which is then dried in the sun. The designs are mainly floral, with names for each scale: buta (large motifs), buti (small), jaal (floral net) and bel (creeper). Peacocks and parrots appear among the creepers, and the usual ground is white or off-white.
Popular writing often describes Bagru as bolder and earthier and Sanganer as lighter and finer. That is a general contrast, not a rule.
artist: Both traditions belong to the Chhipa (Chippa) community. The word is linked to the idea of printing; Incredible India says it comes from chappa, to print. Chhipa families usually handle both dyeing and printing, and carving of blocks is a skill in its own right.
We did not find individually named printers in the pages we read, so we name none. Skills pass inside families, often from father to son and now also to daughters.
Our approach: when the story is told, name the block carvers, dyers and printers, not just the cloth.
place: Bagru is a town in Jaipur district, about 32 km south-west of Jaipur on the Jaipur-Ajmer road, with 31,229 people in the 2011 census. Wikipedia mentions the three-day Jugal Darbar (Lakhi) fair at Bagru, though it gives that detail without a citation.

Sanganer is about 16 km south of Jaipur and is now part of the city's sprawl. It is also known for handmade paper, which Wikipedia traces to Sawai Jai Singh II in 1728, and is a Jain pilgrimage site with the Sanghiji temple.
Dyeing and washing need much clean water, and the towns grew where water and open drying ground were available. Incredible India links Sanganer's prints to the water of the nearby river.

history.what: Incredible India says Chhipa artisans migrated from Gujarat to Bagru, Sanganer and Jahota in this period. Royal families patronised the craft.
Wikipedia says Bagru printing has been part of Rajasthan's textile history for over 400 years. Other sources give shorter figures, so treat this as approximate.
Wikipedia says Sanganer already had an established block-printing base by 1800 and calls its printing tradition roughly 500 years old. These two figures do not agree well, and sources differ.
Sanganeri hand block printing received a Geographical Indication tag.
Wikipedia says Bagru print received a GI tag in 2024. We have not checked the official GI registry.

future: Support clean water and safe wastewater treatment in the printing clusters, so the craft and the towns' rivers and wells both last.
Fund training in block carving, which has few young learners, and protect the carvers' livelihoods.
Keep natural dyes (indigo, madder) viable by helping dye growers and by pricing genuine hand work fairly against machine copies.
Use the GI tags to label real hand-printed cloth, and help artisans, not only traders, to benefit.
Document block patterns and dabu recipes with the printers' names, and keep them in an open archive.

name: Baluchari and Jamdani
tagline: Silk saris that carry whole stories in the pallav, and fine cotton figured by hand.
facts: Baluchari: silk sari with a richly woven pallav, now made at Bishnupur
Baluchari received a GI for West Bengal in 2011
Jamdani: figured cotton muslin woven with a supplementary weft
Dhaniakhali (Hooghly) has its own GI cotton sari, not a Jamdani
art: Baluchari is a silk sari from Bengal. The body is usually plain and the pallav, the end piece, is crowded with woven pictures. Sources describe scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, folk tales and Persian-style designs. Older pieces also show Nawabs, hookah-smoking women and East India Company officers.

Designs are drawn on graph paper, punched onto cards and fed to a jacquard machine. Wikipedia says a sari takes about a week, with two weavers working in shifts. It names three types: resham in a single thread colour, meenakari with two or more colours, and swarnachari with gold or silver zari.

Jamdani is a different cloth. It is a fine cotton muslin with patterns that appear to float on the surface. The pattern is added by hand with extra weft threads, using bamboo sticks and small spools, and is plotted on graph paper placed under the warp. Wikipedia describes it as among the most labour-intensive forms of hand weaving.

Dhaniakhali in Hooghly is often named beside these two. Outlook Traveller describes its saris as sturdy cotton, woven on dobby looms with small repeated geometric designs, and worn as everyday city wear. They hold their own GI (2011). The sources I read do not call them Jamdani.
artist: Baluchari weavers today work around Bishnupur in Bankura district. The sources I read do not name individual weavers working now, so we do not name any.

One name from the revival is well recorded. In the first half of the twentieth century the artist Subho Thakur wanted to revive the craft and introduced the Bishnupur master weaver Akshay Kumar Das to jacquard weaving. Das returned and, with support from Hanuman Das Sarda of the Silk Khadi Seva Mandal, wove Baluchari on local looms.

Live History India names an earlier master, Dubraj of Bhadarpur, who is said to have woven religious texts into saris and signed his work. Jamdani weavers in West Bengal, such as those of Shantipur, are described by Outlook Traveller as people whose families came from Dhaka.
place: Baluchari takes its name from Baluchar, a village near Murshidabad, about 9 km from the old Nawabi capital. Later the work moved to Bishnupur in Bankura, which is now the only place the Wikipedia article calls the home of authentic Baluchari.

Bishnupur's Malla-era terracotta temples are said to have inspired the mythological scenes on the pallav. Shantipur in Nadia and Phulia nearby are textile towns on the Ganga, known for fine cotton, jacquard and Jamdani-style weaving. Dhaniakhali is a block in Hooghly district.

history.what: Sources say Nawab Murshid Quli Khan moved his capital from Dacca to Murshidabad (1704 in Live History India) and brought weavers with him. They settled in Baluchar.
European traders set up silk trade at Cossimbazar, near Murshidabad.
The Baluchar style spread to nearby villages. Then floods, famines and decline in patronage ended the work there, and weavers moved to Bishnupur. Sources differ on exact dates.
Subho Thakur and Akshay Kumar Das bring jacquard weaving to Bishnupur.
Dhaniakhali's handloom hub is said to have begun, as the Outlook Traveller article puts it.
The Bengal famine sets the revival back.
Baluchari and the Dhaniakhali sari each receive a GI tag.
UNESCO lists the traditional art of Jamdani weaving, on a nomination from Bangladesh.

future: Training: pass jacquard design and punch-card skills to young weavers, with paid apprenticeships.
Livelihood: fair prices through cooperatives and direct selling, since a sari takes about a week of two weavers' work.
Materials: Wikipedia notes new Baluchari made with cotton spun with banana and bamboo fibre and natural dyes; this could be developed.
Documentation: record old Baluchar-circle pieces and the names of weavers, as Dubraj signed his work.
Protection: use the GI to keep imitations from carrying the Baluchari name.

name: Banarasi Brocade
tagline: Silk woven with gold and silver thread, in the city on the Ganga where weaving is a way of life.
facts: Form: silk brocade woven with zari (metallic thread)
Loom: handloom, with a Jacquard for the patterns
GI status: 'Banaras Brocades and Sarees', granted in 2009
Six GI districts: Varanasi, Mirzapur, Chandauli, Bhadohi, Jaunpur, Azamgarh
art: Banarasi brocade is silk cloth woven with gold and silver thread, called zari. Zari is not sewn on afterwards. It is woven in as an extra weft, so the metal thread forms the motifs and borders inside the fabric itself. The Incredible India page describes it as a labour-intensive process that needs considerable skill.

The silk is dyed in strong colours and woven on handlooms fitted with a Jacquard, which lifts the warp threads in the order the design needs. Wikipedia lists four main kinds of Banarasi sari: pure silk (katan), organza (kora) with zari and silk, georgette, and shattir. It also lists design techniques such as jangla, tanchoi, vaskat, cutwork, tissue and butidar.

The designs show Mughal and Persian influence. Wikipedia names intertwined flower and leaf motifs such as the kalga and the bel, a row of upright leaves called jhallar along the border, and a net-like pattern called jal. The Indian Culture portal adds a local story that the weavers' first inspiration was the flowers and creepers carved on the Buddhist monuments at Sarnath.
How long a piece takes depends on the design. Wikipedia says from about 15 days to a month, and sometimes up to six months for the most intricate work.
artist: The makers are the weavers of Varanasi and the districts around it, whose skill passes down in families. Wikipedia quotes a Times of India figure that about 1.2 million people are directly or indirectly linked to the handloom silk industry of the region. Counts like this are rough and should be read as estimates.

A Banarasi piece is the work of many hands. Someone draws the design and prepares it for the loom, someone dyes and readies the silk and zari, and the weaver works the loom. The Sahapedia reading list on Varanasi brocades names pattern drawing (nakshabandi) as a craft of its own.

Weavers face pressure from power-loom copies that are faster and cheaper, and from cheaper synthetic yarn. Wikipedia reports that weavers have lost heavily to mechanised units. Varanasi-based labels such as Tilfi Banaras and Ekaya have also begun selling directly to buyers, according to the same article.
place: Varanasi, also called Banaras or Kashi, stands on the Ganga in eastern Uttar Pradesh. It has long been a centre for cotton and silk cloth. The Wikipedia article quotes the English traveller Ralph Fitch, who visited between 1583 and 1591, describing Banaras as a thriving place in the cotton textile trade.

Today brocade weaving is spread over Varanasi and nearby districts. The GI registration covers six: Varanasi, Mirzapur, Chandauli, Bhadohi, Jaunpur and Azamgarh. Only sarees and brocades made there may be sold as Banaras products.
The city's religious life shapes demand. Sarees are a staple of Indian bridal trousseaus and are often kept as family heirlooms, as the Incredible India page notes.

history.what: Some writers trace weaving at Kashi back to the Vedic and Buddhist periods. These claims are repeated in popular sources, and I found no firm documentation for brocade that early.

The traveller Ralph Fitch describes Banaras as a thriving cotton textile centre, as cited by Wikipedia. The earliest mention of Banaras brocade and zari textiles that Wikipedia cites is from the 19th century.

The Incredible India page says brocade weaving is believed to have come to Banaras through Persian artisans, with royal and temple demand helping it grow. Dates differ. Wikipedia also gives the 14th century for the start of gold and silver brocade here, which sits uneasily beside its 17th-century account.
Wikipedia says silk brocade weaving likely began in Banaras after silk weavers moved from Gujarat during the famine of 1603, and grew in excellence over the 18th and 19th centuries.
Weaver associations in Uttar Pradesh apply to the GI Registry in Chennai, with support from UNCTAD, according to Wikipedia's citations.
'Banaras Brocades and Sarees' is granted Geographical Indication status.

Handloom weavers compete with power looms and cheaper yarn. Researchers at IIT-BHU developed natural dyes from plants such as madder, marigold and pomegranate, as Wikipedia reports from a 2007 news item.

future: Training: keep nakshabandi (pattern drawing) and loom skills alive by paying apprentices and master weavers fairly, so young people stay in the trade.
Livelihood: sell more directly to buyers and make GI use easy for small weavers, so that the 'Banaras' name pays the people who actually weave.
Materials: wider use of natural dyes, such as those tried at IIT-BHU, to reduce dye pollution in the Ganga.
Documentation: record patterns, loom set-ups and weaver families.
Protection: enforce the GI against power-loom imitations, and label machine-made cloth honestly.

name: Bandhani
tagline: Thousands of tiny knots tied by hand, so the cloth blooms with dots when the thread is undone.
facts: Form: tie-and-dye resist on cloth; also called bandhej
Name from the Sanskrit bandh, to tie
In Kutch, the work is mostly done by Khatri families
Centres include Bhuj, Mandvi, Anjar, Jamnagar and Rajkot in Gujarat, and towns of Rajasthan
art: In bandhani, small points of cloth are pinched and bound tightly with thread before the cloth is dyed. The tied spots stay undyed and form dots, squares, waves or stripes. Wikipedia notes that the cloth is dyed in stages, moving from lighter to darker shades.

Traditionally the tying was done by hand with the fingernails. The cloth is first washed, bleached, folded and marked with wooden blocks. Named patterns include chandrakala, shikari and khombi. Wikipedia lists main colours as yellow, red, blue, green and black, and says red is linked with marriage and yellow with spring and childbirth, while black and maroon are linked to mourning.

Bandhani is central to wedding dress. Wikipedia mentions the ghar chola given by a mother-in-law. Khamir's exhibition notes say garments have changed from odhanis (shawls) and dresses to saris and shawls in many cloths and prices.
artist: Khamir describes a division of work. Women do the tying, which is the most laborious step. Men generally handle dyeing and the business, though this is not fixed. All Khatri women, it says, are taught tying before they marry.

Most of Kachchh's bandhani artisans are Khatris, some Hindu and some Muslim. Khatris have also been weavers, dyers and block printers, and they practise related resist crafts such as ajrakh. More women from other communities now tie bandhani from home.
We have not found named master artisans in the sources we read. We will add them only when they are properly sourced.
place: In Gujarat the craft is strongest in Kutch and Saurashtra. Khamir names Abdasa, Mandvi, Mundra, Anjar, Bhuj and Nakhatrana as the most active Kachchh centres, each with its own tying and dyeing specialty. Wikipedia says Bhuj is known for its reds, which it partly attributes to local water.

Khatris who moved to Jamnagar, Rajkot and Jaipur became known as Halai Khatris. Wikipedia says production centres are mainly in Rajasthan and Gujarat, and that Rajasthani bandhej differs in colours and designs from the Kutch and Saurashtra work. Our Rajasthan detail here is thin and needs a local source.

history.what: Wikipedia says dyeing at Indus Valley sites may date to around 4000 BCE and that dots may appear in 6th-century paintings at Ajanta. These are suggestions, not firm proof of bandhani.
Wikipedia notes that Banabhatta's Harshacharita mentions a bandhani sari at a royal wedding.
Khamir says King Khengarji I of Kutch (1548-1585) founded or developed several towns and invited settlers from Sindh, many of whom worked in bandhani.
Artisans were employed by the Kutch king and made bandhani for the wealthy and for their own community.
Bandhani moved from local community use to wider markets, and government and NGO support brought exhibitions and exports.

future: Training: bring younger women into tying, with fair pay for slow work.
Livelihood: help home-based tyers earn a fair share, as the work is the hardest step.
Materials: support natural dyes and clean dye houses.
Documentation: record each town's tying and dyeing specialty.
Protection: a Kutch Bandhani GI record exists at the IP India registry, but we did not open it, so check the date and holder there.

name: Bandhej
tagline: Thousands of tiny knots, tied by hand, become a field of dots.
facts: Form: tie-resist dyeing of cloth
Name from 'bandhan', to tie
Centres in Rajasthan: Jaipur, Jodhpur, Sikar, Udaipur, Bikaner
Red is the colour of marriage
art: Bandhej, also called bandhani, is a way of dyeing cloth. Small points of fabric are pinched and tied tightly with thread. The tied spots resist the dye. When the thread is removed, dots appear against the coloured ground.

Aza Fashions describes the steps. The cloth is washed and bleached, and designs are stamped with a temporary dye. Tying begins, and dyeing starts with the lightest shade, often yellow. More tying and darker baths follow. The cloth is crinkled where it was tied, and the texture eases when ironed.

Patterns have names. Aza lists ekdali (single dot), boond (dot with a dark centre), khas-khas (very fine dots), chandrakala (moon phases) and bavan baug (a grid of gardens). Aza says red is linked with marriage and love, and yellow with spring and joy.
Isha's Save the Weave says saris, odhnis and turbans are the usual products, and that a pattern can show membership of a community.
artist: Aza Fashions says women traditionally do the tying, often with a pointed ring worn on the finger, the nakhuna, while men usually handle the dyeing.

Several sources link the Khatri community to the craft. Isha says the Khatri of Gujarat are credited with starting bandhani in India. Sources differ on where it began, so this is best read as a tradition.
place: In Rajasthan the main centres named by Aza and Isha are Jaipur, Jodhpur, Sikar, Udaipur and Bikaner, with Bhilwara and Ajmer also listed by Isha. Gujarat has its own centres, such as Jamnagar and Kutch.
Leheriya, the wave-striped tied cloth, is a related but separate Rajasthani technique.

history.what: Aza says the technique goes back nearly 5,000 years. I found no scholarly source in my reading that confirms that figure.
Isha cites dotted cloth in the Ajanta caves as an early picture of tie-dye.
Aza cites a mention of a bandhej sari at a royal wedding in Banabhatta's Harshacharita.
Aza says it was favoured by royalty and tied to celebration and prestige.

future: Pay fair rates for the tying, which is slow and often home-based.
Train young tiers and dyers in both fine and new designs.
Promote hand-tied work over printed imitation dots.
Support safe, good-quality dyes and clean water use.
Document pattern names and their meanings.

name: Bhadohi Carpets
tagline: Hand-knotted wool carpets from the lanes of a small district near Varanasi.
facts: Method: knots tied by hand on vertical looms
Density: from 30 to over 400 knots per square inch
Yarns: wool, cotton, silk
GI: Bhadohi carpets, 2010
art: Bhadohi carpets are hand-knotted. Weavers tie each knot by hand on a vertical loom. PARI reports densities from 30 to 300 knots per square inch, and a producer's page says a single premium carpet can reach 425. The yarns are wool, cotton and silk.
A producer's page says a weaver ties roughly 6,000 to 9,000 knots a day. PARI says the methods have changed little in at least two centuries.

Production is a cottage industry. The looms stand in homes across villages and towns, and a company coordinates weavers by sending production officers round to the looms. The carpets are mostly for export. PARI reports that about 90 per cent of Indian carpets are exported, with the United States taking over half.
artist: The weavers are rural families, many of them women, and skills pass from parents to children. PARI speaks with Akhtar Ali, a weaver in his forties who has taken up tailoring because carpet income has fallen, and Urmila Prajapati, 45, who stopped weaving because of falling income and eye problems and plans to resume.

PARI estimates that the industry supports nearly two million rural artisans. A producer's page says the trade supports more than 100,000 people in an extended family. These counts differ widely, so treat them as rough.
Cheaper machine-made copies, especially from China, press hard on the weavers. PARI notes that the GI tag has not improved weavers' business.
place: Bhadohi is a small district in eastern Uttar Pradesh, near Varanasi and next to Mirzapur. A producer's page calls it India's oldest carpet-weaving hub and says it makes over 60 per cent of the country's rugs. This figure is the company's claim and I have not seen it confirmed independently.
The belt of Bhadohi and Mirzapur lies between the old trade routes of the Grand Trunk Road and the weaving city of Varanasi. The same belt is part of the GI area for Banaras brocades.
The carpet clusters sit in villages and small towns, with looms in family homes.

history.what: Popular accounts say hand-knotted carpets came to this region under Emperor Akbar, and the weaving centres at Bhadohi and Mirzapur grew out of that. PARI and a producer's page both repeat this. I found no primary document, so it is a traditional account.
Mass production of handmade woollen pile carpets begins in the Bhadohi region (PARI).
Mubarak Ali and Sons is founded, later exporting to the UK, US, EU and Japan. It closed in 2016 after orders fell, according to PARI.
Bhadohi carpets receive a Geographical Indication.
India's carpet exports are worth $2.23 billion, of which handmade carpets are $1.51 billion (PARI).

future: Training: bring young people back to the loom with fair pay, since many weavers are leaving for other work.
Livelihood: raise weavers' share of the price and sell hand-knotted work as hand-knotted, away from machine copies.
Materials and health: better lighting at looms, since PARI mentions eye problems among weavers.
Documentation: record designs, knot counts and weaver families.
Protection: make the GI mean something on the ground, which PARI says it has not yet done for weavers.

name: Bhotia Woollens
tagline: Rugs, blankets and shawls woven by Bhotia women from the wool of their own sheep.
facts: Makers: Bhotia (Bhotiya) women of Kumaon and Garhwal
Pieces: dann rugs, thulma blankets, pankhi shawls, chutka
Bhotia dann has held GI status since 2021, per Incredible India
Wool from the community's own sheep
art: The Bhotia of the upper Himalayan valleys of Kumaon and Garhwal have long reared sheep. Incredible India says the wool goes into dann, a hand-knotted rug woven on a wooden frame by women.
The chamoli.gov.in page lists other pieces: thulma (a bedspread), chutka, asan, pankhi (a shawl), carpets, and others. Women wove them on a small loom called pithachan.

Incredible India describes the dann process: wool is washed, dyed with natural colours such as indigo and madder, warped, woven and knotted to form the pile, then trimmed, washed and sun-dried. Sources say synthetic dyes have largely replaced natural ones.

Motifs include geometric forms for mountains and rivers, flowers and animals of the Himalaya, and some designs from Buddhist and Chinese art. One source says some motifs show Tibetan, Nepali and Chinese influence while keeping a local character.
artist: Women are the main weavers. Wikipedia says home-based wool work employs many Bhotia women, who gather plants for natural dyes. Designs are passed down through generations.

Munsiyari is known for dunn rugs and thulma bedspreads, and Dunda for carpets and pashmina shawls. In the Dunda area, weavers work through winter and sell at seasonal fairs and tourist sites in summer.
The sources I read do not name individual weavers.
place: The Bhotia live in the high valleys of Chamoli, Pithoragarh and Uttarkashi, and are described as semi-nomadic pastoralists who moved across the India-Tibet borderlands. The Chamoli district page places the Bhotiya of the Mana and Niti valleys and their trade with Tibet at the root of their wool work.
Wool comes from the community's sheep, grazed on high pastures such as Harsil.

history.what: The Chamoli district page says trade with Tibet made wool central to Bhotiya life. No dates are given.
Incredible India says dann weaving began about a century ago, when Johari women from Pithoragarh went to Tarikhet in Almora district to learn it. Other sources describe the craft as older.
Incredible India says Bhotia dann has held Geographical Indication status since 2021.
Weavers sell at fairs and to visitors. Sources say synthetic dyes have largely replaced natural dyes.

future: Training: teach younger women pit loom and dann knotting, with natural dyeing.
Livelihood: direct sales at fairs and online, so weavers keep a fair share of the price.
Materials: revive natural dyes where possible, and secure grazing rights for the sheep.
Documentation: record motifs, local names and weaver families.
Protection: use the GI to separate hand-knotted Bhotia dann from machine copies.

name: Bodo Aronai Weaving
tagline: A narrow scarf, woven by Bodo women, that carries the honour of a guest.
facts: Aronai: a woven scarf used to honour guests and elders
Patterns made by extra-weft weaving
Throw-shuttle loom
Bodo Aronai received a GI tag in October 2024
art: The aronai is a traditional ceremonial scarf of the Bodo people. Bharatpedia gives its size as roughly 1.5 to 2.5 metres long and 25 to 50 cm wide. The Sentinel describes it as a small cloth used as a scarf on festive occasions, a symbol of Bodo culture given to honour and welcome guests.
It sits within a set of Bodo dress. Wikipedia's Dokhona article lists the dokhona wrap worn by women, a shoulder cloth, and the aronai worn by men and women on special occasions.

Patterns are made by extra-weft weaving, where extra coloured threads are added during weaving. The IIAD article names motifs drawn from nature and daily life, such as the fern (dinghkiya bibar), peacock's glance (dawrei mekhrep), turtle shell (kasau bikha), floating water hyacinth (bwigri bibar) and pigeon's eye (phareo megon). These are woven patterns, called agor. Colours are bright: reds, yellows and greens are common.
artist: Weaving is women's work among the Bodo. IIAD says women weave the family's garments, and the craft supports both household needs and income. Skills are passed down within families.

Weavers use a throw-shuttle loom with a bamboo reed, healds and treadles, per IIAD. The same article says yarn is washed and dyed before warping. It notes the Aagor initiative supports over 100 women artisans.
IIAD lists problems the weavers face: few cooperatives, old looms, high transport costs, limited finance and little exposure to markets.
place: The Bodo live mainly in the Bodoland Territorial Region of Assam, north of the Brahmaputra. Looms are found in many homes.

The Sentinel reported on 3 October 2024 that eight Bodo items, including the aronai, got GI tags from the Registry in Chennai, announced by Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma and Bodoland Territorial Council head Pramod Boro.

history.what: Bharatpedia says the scarf was sometimes presented to respected people or warriors as a mark of recognition. This is from a community wiki and is not independently confirmed.
Bodo Aronai receives a Geographical Indication tag, reported 3 October 2024.

future: Training: teach young women the extra-weft patterns and their names.
Livelihood: build cooperatives and common facility centres, as IIAD recommends.
Materials: set up yarn depots for steady supply; keep plant dyes alive.
Documentation: record every motif with its Bodo name and meaning, from weavers themselves.
Protection: use the GI tag so only genuine Bodo-woven cloth is sold as Bodo Aronai.

name: Chamba Rumal
tagline: An embroidered cloth with no wrong side, where a painter's drawing is worked in silk on both faces.
facts: Form: hand embroidery on muslin or khaddar, made by women
Stitch: double satin stitch (do rukha tanka), identical on both sides
Themes: Rasamandala, Gita Govinda, Ragamala, Ramayana
GI registered; sources differ on the date (2007 or 2010)
art: A Chamba rumal is a square of embroidered cloth. A rumal was traditionally a cover for gifts or for festival offerings, and it was a common gift at weddings. The best work looks like a Pahari miniature painting done in thread.

Its signature is the double satin stitch, called do rukha tanka. Each stitch is worked so that the picture looks the same on both faces and the cloth has no wrong side. Bandi tanka, a stem stitch, outlines figures and borders.

The cloth is unbleached muslin, or mulmul, or khaddar. Miniature-style work uses untwisted silk thread, or silver-gilt thread. A painter first draws the design with a charcoal or fine brush. Older threads were dyed with madder and indigo, using alum as a mordant. A border of about two to four inches frames the piece.

Themes come from the same world as Pahari painting. Rasamandala shows Krishna on a lotus with dancing gopis around him. Other rumals follow the Gita Govinda, the Ragamala, the Ramayana, Rukmini Haran and local festivals.
artist: The embroiderers are women. The designs were drawn by painters, and men from the Manikanth family and others such as Prem Lal and Hans Raj are named as master sketchers who supervised the work.

Sources name modern embroiderers including Suraj Begum, Rajinder Kumari Nayyar, Lalita Vakil and Masto Devi. Lalita Vakil received the Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2018 for organising courses to revive the art.

The earliest reported rumal is said to be one made by Bebe Nanaki, sister of Guru Nanak, in the 16th century, kept in a gurdwara at Hoshiarpur. This is a tradition reported by Wikipedia and I did not find a second source.
place: Chamba is a hill town on the Ravi river. Tradition says Raja Sahil Varman moved the capital there around 920 CE and named it for his daughter Champavati. Chamba was largely independent for about a thousand years and joined India in 1948.

Chamba rumals are kept in the Himachal State Museum, the National Museum in New Delhi, Bharat Kala Bhavan at Banaras Hindu University and other museums. The Bhuri Singh Museum in Chamba holds Pahari paintings of the same world.

history.what: The earliest reported rumal, by Bebe Nanaki, is dated here (tradition).
Pahari art flourishes in Chamba through exchange with Basohli, Kangra and Nurpur; women of Chamba embroider rumals as wedding gifts.
Miniature-style rumals appear under Raja Umed Singh and Raja Jit Singh, when royal women took an interest.
Royal patronage ends and the craft declines.
Usha Bhagat leads a search for old designs in museums; women are trained and 16 designs are recreated.
The Delhi Crafts Council begins a revival.
The CHARU training centre opens in Chamba on 3 April.
GI registration; sources differ.

future: Training: keep centres such as CHARU running and pay trainers and trainees fairly.
Livelihood: direct sale to buyers, so embroiderers, not middlemen, earn from a piece that takes months.
Materials: support supply of fine muslin and silk thread, and natural dyes for older-style work.
Documentation: photograph and catalogue old rumals in museums and record the stitches.
Protection: use the GI mark so machine-made copies cannot be sold as Chamba rumal.

name: Chanderi and Maheshwari Weaving
tagline: Two towns, two light handloom saris: sheer Chanderi on the Malwa-Bundelkhand edge, and reversible-bordered Maheshwari on the Narmada.
facts: Chanderi: silk, cotton or silk-cotton, with zari; GI tag in 2005 (per Fashion Law Journal)
Maheshwari: traditionally cotton, now also silk warp with cotton weft
Chanderi motifs: coins, flowers, peacocks
Maheshwari motifs: fort walls, Narmada waves (lahariya), flowers
art: Madhya Pradesh has two well-known handloom saris that are often named together. Chanderi is woven in Chanderi town in Ashoknagar district. Maheshwari is woven in Maheshwar, on the Narmada in Khargone district. Both are light and made for hot summers.

Chanderi cloth is sheer, with a soft sheen. Weavers make it in pure silk, Chanderi cotton and silk-cotton. The Incredible India page says the sarees are often decorated with gold and silver zari, and that common motifs are coins, flowers and peacocks. A Fashion Law Journal article says mill-made yarn replaced hand-spun yarn in the 1890s, and Japanese silk began to be used for the warp in the 1930s. Another source gives 1945 for the silk, so the date is not settled.

Maheshwari saris were first made of finely hand-spun cotton, about nine yards long, with a pallu at both ends. When one end frayed, the sari could be turned and worn again. The Madhya Pradesh Tourism page says the body is usually plain, while the border and pallu carry the design. The pallu has five stripes. Designs are said to come from the Maheshwar fort walls, the Narmada's waves, and flowers such as aak and chameli.
Today Maheshwari fabric is also made as silk-cotton, and as scarves, stoles and dress material. A premium sari can take more than fifteen days to make, according to Outlook Traveller.
artist: Sources name weaving communities rather than individual masters. For Chanderi, Wikipedia attributes the tradition to Koli weavers, and one retailer-linked source also names the Momin community. Accounts differ, so this is best treated as indicative. The Fashion Law Journal says the Scindia family patronised Chanderi in the early twentieth century, and that cooperatives and training programmes helped weavers after independence.

For Maheshwar, the Rehwa Society is the name most often given in the revival. Madhya Pradesh Tourism says Richard and Sally Holkar founded it in 1979. Outlook Traveller gives 1978, so sources differ by a year. Wikipedia says it employs about 130 weavers, while Outlook Traveller mentions about 70 looms across four units; these numbers are from different dates and should be checked.

The Fashion Law Journal lists the pressures on Chanderi weavers. They are competition from machine-made cloth, uneven demand, low and unsteady income, and young people's reluctance to take up weaving.
place: Chanderi is a heritage town in Ashoknagar district. The Incredible India page says it dates to the 11th century and was held in turn by Rajput rulers, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals. It is known for its fort, the Kati Ghati gateway, the Badal Mahal Gate and the Chanderi Museum. It also has a Chanderi Handloom Park where visitors can watch weaving. The nearest railway station is Lalitpur, about 40 km away.

Maheshwar lies on the northern bank of the Narmada in Khargone district. Wikipedia says it was a Holkar capital of Malwa until the capital moved to Indore in 1818. Ahilya Fort, built under Ahilyabai Holkar, overlooks the river and is now a heritage hotel. Weavers work in the town's looms and in Rehwa Society units near the fort.

history.what: Wikipedia says Chanderi's weaving culture emerged in this period. Other sources give later dates, so the age is uncertain.
Trade between Malwa, Gujarat and central India increased the importance of Chanderi (Incredible India; Wikipedia).
Wikipedia links the sari tradition to Koli weavers, and gives both the 13th century and about 1350.
Ahilyabai Holkar rules from Maheshwar. Madhya Pradesh Tourism says she invited weavers from Malwa and Gujarat; another source says from Mandu.
Mill-made yarn replaces hand-spun yarn at Chanderi (Fashion Law Journal).
Japanese silk begins to be used for Chanderi warp, per the same source.
Richard and Sally Holkar found the Rehwa Society to revive Maheshwari weaving; sources differ on the year.
Chanderi receives a Geographical Indication tag (Fashion Law Journal).

future: Training: Chanderi's young people are reluctant to weave. Paid apprenticeships and weaving schools, like the Rehwa school at Maheshwar, can help.
Livelihood: fair wages and direct sales through handloom parks and cooperatives lessen the pull of power looms.
Materials: reliable supplies of fine cotton and silk yarn, and of natural dyes, keep the cloth's character.
Documentation: record the weavers' names, patterns and loom techniques, which the sources I read mostly leave unnamed.
Protection: the Chanderi GI tag is useful only if buyers can check authenticity, for example by tags and registered weaver lists.

name: Chikankari
tagline: White thread on fine cloth, the whisper embroidery of Awadh.
facts: Medium: muslin, cotton, georgette, silk
Technique: hand embroidery, shadow work
Stitches: bakhiya, tepchi, jali, murri and many more
art: Chikankari is a delicate hand embroidery from Lucknow. Traditionally white thread is worked on white or pale fabric. There are dozens of stitches: bakhiya (shadow work, stitched on the back so that the pattern shows through the cloth), tepchi, jali (a lace-like openwork) and murri, among others.
The motifs are floral and vine patterns, often drawn from Mughal design. A pattern is first block-printed on the cloth, then embroidered and the print is washed out.
artist: Most Chikankari is stitched by women working at home in Lucknow and surrounding villages, often paid by the piece. Block-makers, printers, washers and finishers each contribute.
Many embroiderers earn very little compared with the final retail price, so fair pay is the craft's central question.
Our approach: trace each garment back to its stitcher and share the price chain.
place: Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh, was the seat of the Nawabs of Awadh, patrons of music, poetry, cuisine and textiles. Its culture is known as tehzeeb.
The craft lives in the old city's markets and in outlying villages such as Malihabad.

history.what: A popular story credits the Mughal empress Noor Jahan with introducing the craft, though historians treat this as tradition rather than proof.
Under the Nawabs of Awadh, Lucknow became a centre of fine embroidery.
Demand fell after the loss of royal patrons, then recovered through the garment market.
Chikankari is a fashion staple, and machine imitations are common.

future: Fair pay: publish what the stitcher earns per piece and encourage buyers to pay for it.
Hand-made labelling so buyers can tell real chikankari from machine copies.
Train a new generation, including men and women, in the full range of stitches.

name: Eri (Ryndia) Silk
tagline: Silk spun from cocoons the moth has already left, woven by village women on bamboo looms.
facts: Local name: ryndia; the worm feeds on castor leaves
Called ahimsa silk because the cocoon is not boiled with the pupa inside
Ri-Bhoi is a main centre of eri weaving
Ryndia received a GI tag in April 2025, per a government press release
art: Eri silk comes from silkworms that feed on castor plants. In Meghalaya it is called ryndia. The V&A guest post says the silk is taken from the cocoon without killing the larva, so it is called ahimsa, or non-violent, silk. The yarn is spun by hand and dyed with natural dyes.

The cloth is woven on traditional floor looms made entirely of bamboo, including the reed that beats the cloth. Village women make the looms and their parts by hand. Frame looms are also used now to raise output. A floor loom makes one scarf for each warp that is set up.

Eri cloth is used for the shawls (jainkup) and wraps (jainpein) of Khasi dress. The V&A post describes the traditional Shella jainpein as a red and yellow square check. Woven eri shawls also serve as the base cloth for Khneng embroidery, which uses geometric patterns in black wool and is practised in Mustoh and the Shella region.
Meghalaya produces three silks: eri, muga and mulberry. Eri is the one most tied to Ri-Bhoi.
artist: Spinning and weaving in Meghalaya are largely women's work, unlike much of India where men dominate these crafts. The V&A post says the work helps women, including elders and young mothers, earn while staying close to home. Skills pass down through families, and many weavers also farm.

The same post names two women. Kong Kwickstar Tmung of Diwon learned natural dyeing and weaving from her mother and now teaches others. Kong Loin Nongpoh of Umtnang, an elderly weaver, mainly rears and spins silk now. Khneng embroidery was practised by only three women until early 2015, and nine more began learning after training, according to the same post.

A press report on the May 2026 opening of an eri yarn unit at Bhoirymbong says Ri-Bhoi has about 7,200 eri farmers, nearly 60 tonnes of cocoons and about 1,000 weavers. I read only the search summary of that report, so treat the numbers with care.
place: Ri-Bhoi district lies north of Shillong. The V&A post calls it a main centre of eri culture and handloom weaving in Meghalaya, with all materials sourced locally. Traders carried eri base cloth woven in Ri-Bhoi to embroiderers in Mustoh, and the embroidery reflects those old trade routes.
Umden-Diwon in Ri-Bhoi was declared the state's first Eri Silk Village in 2021, according to news summaries. The Shella region in the south Khasi Hills uses eri in its traditional dress.

history.what: Sources I read do not give a firm date for when eri rearing began in Meghalaya. Ri-Bhoi is described as long established.
Eri cloth woven in Ri-Bhoi travels to Mustoh and Shella, where it becomes part of local dress and embroidery.
The Indigenous Terra Madre event in Meghalaya showcases eri, with NESFAS, the state sericulture and weaving department and GIZ involved.
Umden-Diwon is declared Meghalaya's first Eri Silk Village, per news summaries.
Traditional Ryndia receives a GI tag, per a government press release. A Wikipedia entry gives registration numbers, but I could not check them.
A news report says the Chief Minister gifted a ryndia fabric to the Prime Minister, which drew national attention to the cloth.
A first eri yarn manufacturing unit in Ri-Bhoi is reported, per press coverage.

future: Training: older weavers like Kong Kwickstar Tmung already teach natural dyeing and weaving. More paid teaching roles would help.
Livelihood: the GI tag and local yarn spinning units can help weavers earn more. Fair prices matter, as weaving is fitted around farm work.
Materials: castor plants and natural dye plants need to stay available locally. Frame looms raise output but should not replace bamboo floor looms entirely.
Documentation: patterns of Shella and Khneng work, and the names of weaving families, are not fully recorded.
Protection: the GI tag works only if sellers use it honestly. Weavers need help to prove their cloth is genuine ryndia.

name: Gadwal Sarees
tagline: A cotton body joined to a silk and zari border so finely that the seam is hard to find.
facts: Form: cotton body, silk border, zari pallu
Technique: kuttu, a three-shuttle interlocked weft
GI registered; the registry lists 4 August 2010
Often described as very light
art: A Gadwal saree is made in three parts. The body is cotton, the border is silk and the pallu is silk with zari. They are joined on the loom, not stitched, using an interlocked weft called kuttu. Aditya Birla's Kaarigari feature describes this as a three-shuttle weave that binds the three fabrics thread by thread.
The result is a saree that is light, and Wikipedia says it can be packed into a matchbox. Gadwal sarees are sold in cotton and in silk versions, so the material varies by product.
Wikipedia notes a custom linked to Tirupati: the Brahmotsavam begins with the deity's idol adorned with a Gadwal saree. Kaarigari writes that the saree began as a textile woven for temples.
artist: Kaarigari says women from the local weaving community do almost all of the work, from spinning and preparing cotton thread to setting up looms. It does not name the community.

The same feature says market demand moved towards silk, speed and volume, and weavers were pushed to give up cotton and the three-shuttle method. It describes a revival by Aadyam Handwoven that offers fair pay to weavers.

Wikipedia credits the Gadwal Handloom Centre, set up in 1946 by Ratan Babu Rao, with spreading knowledge of the saree. The GI applicant is the Rajoli Handloom Weavers Cooperative Productions Sales Society Ltd.
place: Gadwal is in Jogulamba Gadwal district, Telangana. The district takes its name from the Jogulamba temple at Alampur.
Kaarigari says Gadwal Samsthanam was a vassal of the Nizam of Hyderabad, and that King Somanadri built a fort in the 17th century.

history.what: King Somanadri builds a fort at Gadwal, according to the Kaarigari feature.
Some accounts put the saree at about 200 years old. This is not firmly documented.
Gadwal Handloom Centre is established by Ratan Babu Rao, per Wikipedia.
The GI registry lists Gadwal Sarees (application 137) with this certificate date.
Weavers shift to silk; revival work supports the cotton and kuttu method.

future: Training: teach kuttu weaving to younger weavers, as the three-shuttle method is the part most at risk.
Livelihood: fair, steady pay and direct buyers.
Materials: support fine cotton yarn and silk supply.
Documentation: record kuttu step by step with the weavers.
Protection: use the GI and clear labels for handloom against powerloom.

name: Himroo
tagline: A cotton-and-silk cloth woven to look like royal gold brocade.
facts: Form: patterned fabric with silk motifs on a cotton or wool base
Made in Aurangabad
Linked to Mohammad Tughlaq's 14th-century move to Daulatabad
Listed as GI protected on Sahapedia
art: Himroo is a patterned cloth from Aurangabad. Aza Fashions describes a cotton or wool base with motifs woven in silk using a discontinuous weft, where small spools of silk form the design. The article calls it a second-class brocade because it imitates costly silk and gold fabrics with simpler materials.

Sahapedia describes extra-weft weaving on a throw-shuttle loom, with cotton and viscose rayon or silk with gold thread, and says the design must be fixed at the start. Sources disagree on the exact materials.

The designs draw on flowers such as the lotus, fruits, birds, geometric patterns and architecture. Wikipedia says the name may come from the Persian hum-ruh, similar, and that it echoes kinkhwab, the gold and silver cloth of royal families.
artist: We found little reliable material naming Himroo weavers or their communities, so this section is brief. Aza Fashions says handwoven Himroo is now rare, because power looms make similar cloth faster, producers use rayon and chemical dyes, and fewer young artisans take up the craft.

The same article notes that designers and government bodies are working to support the remaining weavers. We could not read the Counterview piece on the weavers' lanes, so we do not describe their daily life here.
place: Himroo is tied to Aurangabad in Maharashtra, close to Daulatabad. Sahapedia lists Aurangabad as its region and gives the GI status as protected. Another source puts the GI tag at 2008, which we could not confirm in the GI registry.
Aza Fashions links the designs to the nearby caves at Ajanta and Ellora, a connection the article asserts without evidence. Treat it as a popular view.

history.what: Wikipedia and Aza Fashions tie Himroo to Mohammad Tughlaq's move of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad. Weavers came with the court and many stayed. Historians have not proved a Persian origin.
Sahapedia dates Himroo to this century and links it to Persian origins and the Deccan sultanates.
Wikipedia says the craft flourished under Malik Ambar and in the Mughal period.
Handweaving shrinks as power looms and rayon spread (Aza Fashions).

future: Training: apprenticeships for young weavers.
Livelihood: market links for authentic handwoven Himroo, not power-loom copies.
Materials: support to use silk and cotton rather than only rayon.
Documentation: record motifs, looms and the names of the remaining weaving families.
Protection: confirm the GI status and enforce it with labels.

name: Ilkal Sarees
tagline: A cotton body looped to a silk pallu with the tope teni join, woven only at Ilkal looms.
facts: Place: Ilkal, Bagalkot district
Technique: kondi weft and tope teni pallu join
Cotton body with art silk or silk border and pallu
GI tag; sources give 2006 or 2007
art: An Ilkal saree has a cotton body and a silk pallu. The two are woven as one cloth. The warp of the body is joined to the warp of the pallu by a looping method called tope teni. The Incredible India page says each saree is woven from scratch and not stitched from sections, and Wikipedia says the method is used only at Ilkal.

The weft goes in through a method called kondi. Wikipedia says three shuttles are used with two contrasting colours. The pallu is classically red silk with white patterns that look like temple towers. In Wikipedia's account the traditional design is tope teni seragu, with three red sections divided by white.

Borders have their own names. Incredible India lists gomi (also called Ilkal dadi), paraspet and gaadi. Colours include pomegranate red, peacock green, parrot green, indigo and mustard. The body may be plain or striped, or have squares and rectangles. Some sarees also carry Kasuti embroidery with palanquins, elephants and lotuses.
Yarn combinations vary. Wikipedia lists silk with silk, silk with cotton, and art silk with cotton. Incredible India mentions cotton and viscose for the body, and silk for the pallu.
artist: Ilkal weaving is a household trade. Wikipedia says women of the family take an active part, and that a saree takes around seven days on a handloom. A weaver works with two helpers on preparation, according to Incredible India.
Wikipedia gives a figure of about 20,000 people in saree weaving at Ilkal. I did not find the number confirmed in an official census, so treat it as approximate.
The sources I read do not name individual master weavers.
place: Ilkal is a town in a valley in the south-east of Bagalkot district, in northern Karnataka. Incredible India says the sarees are made at 25 weaving centres across four districts of the state.
Visitors to Ilkal can also see the Kallur Siddeshwara temple and the Banashankari temple, both named on the Incredible India page. Shops in the town sell the sarees directly.

history.what: Many people believe weaving at Ilkal began in the 8th century CE. Wikipedia and Incredible India repeat this, but no document is cited for it.
The Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency (1884) records 684 looms at Ilkal in 1883. It is the earliest official record given by Incredible India.
Ilkal sarees receive a GI tag. Incredible India gives 2006. Other sources I only saw as search snippets give 2007.
Handlooms share the town with power looms. A Gulf News report cited in a search result says weavers saw little extra business from the GI tag.

future: Training: teach tope teni and kondi to young weavers while masters are still working.
Livelihood: pay handloom prices that reflect seven days of work, and keep the GI mark meaningful against power-loom copies.
Materials: secure steady supplies of good cotton and silk yarn for the 25 centres.
Documentation: record border and pallu designs, and the names of weaving families.
Protection: label sarees clearly as handloom or power loom.

name: Kalamkari
tagline: Painting and printing with the pen, in colours from roots and leaves.
facts: Medium: cotton and silk
Dyes: indigo, madder, myrobalan, iron-jaggery
Tools: bamboo kalam; carved wood blocks
art: Kalamkari means 'pen work'. Two schools are best known: Srikalahasti, where artists freehand temple narratives with a kalam, and Machilipatnam, where carved wooden blocks print floral and vine patterns, with Persian influence.
The cloth goes through many steps: treated with myrobalan and buffalo milk, outlined, mordanted, dyed, and washed repeatedly in running water. A single piece can take weeks.
artist: Srikalahasti was a temple town and its painters, who drew scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas, worked in artisan families. Machilipatnam's printers and dyers were woven into the old port's trade.
In the 20th century, Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay's efforts helped revive the craft after it declined against synthetic prints.
Our approach: document each step and who does it, from the dyer to the painter.
place: Srikalahasti, on the Swarnamukhi river, is a pilgrim town centred on the Vayu linga temple. Machilipatnam is a historic port on the Bay of Bengal, once a hub of the Golconda and European cloth trade.
Clean running water is as vital to the craft as colour. River pollution and drought are direct threats.

history.what: Indian painted and printed cottons were traded across Asia and beyond.
Under the Golconda sultanate, Machilipatnam's printed cloth was a key export; Persian motifs entered the style.
Cheap mill-printed fabric and synthetic dyes hit the craft badly.
Revival through government and craft-board work; today it is a popular fashion textile.

future: Clean water first: support river and effluent monitoring with the dyers who depend on it.
Keep natural dyes viable by sharing recipes and buying their output fairly.
Teach the pen: make the freehand Srikalahasti skill an attractive career for young people.
