name: Kanchipuram Silk
tagline: A heavy mulberry silk saree where the border and the body are woven apart and locked together.
facts: Form: handwoven mulberry silk saree with zari
GI: registered 2 June 2005 (TNDALU report)
Signature: contrast border and pallu joined by interlocking
A single saree can take 15 to 20 days (TNDALU report)
art: The Kanchipuram saree, also called Kanjeevaram, is woven in pure mulberry silk with zari, a thread of silver coated with gold. It is known for wide borders in a colour that contrasts with the body, and for its weight.

A TNDALU field report describes the loom work. Three shuttles are used. One weaver works the right side while an aide works the left. The body and border are woven separately and then interlocked. The report says the joint is so strong that the border will not come away even if the saree tears. The hanging end, the mundhi, is often woven in another shade and joined, and the join is often marked by a zigzag line.
Before weaving, the threads are dipped in rice water and dried in the sun to keep the cloth firm. The report says the fabric is heavy because three to four strands of silk are used.

Traditional designs include temple borders, checks, stripes and floral buttas. Some mundhis show scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata or paintings associated with Raja Ravi Varma. Designs are held on punched design cards that weavers follow; the report says chips may replace them.
artist: The weavers are mainly from the Devanga and Saliyar (Saligar) communities, according to a retailer's history page. Dyers, winders, designers and zari workers are part of the same chain, and their names are rarely recorded.

The TNDALU report, based on a visit to Kanchipuram in April 2023, says many weavers earn little, while the saree sells for several times what the weaver is paid. Some traditional weaving families have stopped weaving. Many weavers and dyers it spoke to did not know about the GI tag.
Our approach: name the weaving families and the cooperatives, and show the dyers and the aide at the loom, not only the finished saree.
place: Kanchipuram is a temple town in northern Tamil Nadu. Its weaving is tied to the temples around it, and the temple architecture has long been a source of saree motifs. A TNDALU field report names the yali (an elephant-lion creature), the ganda berunda (a two-headed bird) and the temple border called reku.

The silk comes from South India, though the field report also says dyed silk is often brought from Surat and other states. The same report says the zari is from Gujarat in one place and from South India in another, so sources differ on where it is made. Weaving happens in homes and workshops, and in co-operative societies. The first co-operative, Kamatchi Amman, is said to date from 1942.
The report cites about 60,000 weavers and 60,000 looms, while Wikipedia, citing 2008, says about 5,000 families. These numbers differ a great deal, so treat all of them as rough.

history.what: Retail and blog pages tell stories linking the craft to the sage Markanda and to a mention by the grammarian Patanjali. These are traditions without sourcing, and one page dates the weavers' arrival to the Chola king Raja Raja. No scholarly source I read confirms any of this.
The Kamatchi Amman co-operative society, said to be the first Kanchipuram silk co-operative, was set up at Kanchipuram (TNDALU report).
The saree was registered as a Geographical Indication. The report says it was the second GI from Tamil Nadu. Wikipedia gives 2005-06.
The Tamil film Kanchivaram, about the weavers' struggles, was released (Wikipedia).
A law university report found that only one authorised user had registered under the GI, and that the co-operative seal itself was being copied.

future: Help weavers become registered authorised users of the GI, so that the tag protects them and not only the sellers.
Pay fair wages and share the sale price more fairly between weaver, dyer and shop.
Keep handloom weaving alive for families who want it, and label machine-made copies honestly.
Document the design cards, motifs and the roles of every worker in the chain, with the weavers' own words.
Look at safer dyeing for the workers, who handle hot water and chemicals all day.

name: Kani & Pashmina
tagline: Fine mountain goat wool, spun by hand and woven in a pattern of wooden bobbins.
facts: Medium: fine wool from the Changthangi goat
Technique: hand-spinning and handloom weaving
Kani: woven with small wooden bobbins
art: Pashmina is a very fine wool from the underbelly of the Changthangi goat, which lives on the high plateau of Ladakh. The fibre is spun by hand and woven into shawls of feather-light warmth.
Kani shawls are the most elaborate. Patterns are woven in using many small wooden bobbins called kanis, one for each colour. A single shawl can take months or even years.
artist: Spinning is traditionally done by women at home, weaving by men on handlooms, with embroiderers adding detail. Many weavers work in Srinagar's old city and in Kanihama village in Budgam.
Pashmina is both an heirloom and a livelihood.
Our approach: the story of every shawl begins with the herder and the spinner.
place: Kashmir's valley, ringed by the Himalaya, is joined with Ladakh's high plateau, where Changpa herders raise the goats.
Srinagar, on the Jhelum river, is the centre of the trade.

history.what: Tradition credits Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin with bringing weavers to Kashmir from Central Asia.
Kashmir shawls became a luxury in Mughal, Sikh and European markets.
Machine-made fakes are a threat, and Kani weaving has a geographical-indication label.

future: Testing and labelling to stop fakes.
Fair prices for herders and spinners.
Preserve kani pattern books and train young weavers.

name: Kantha
tagline: Old saris stitched into new stories, one running stitch at a time.
facts: Medium: layered old cotton cloth
Stitch: running stitch
Subject: flowers, fish, boats, village life
art: Kantha is a way of making new cloth from old. Worn saris and dhotis are layered and sewn together with a simple running stitch, which also gathers the cloth into a gentle ripple. Over this base, embroiderers stitch borders and pictures: lotuses, fish, trees, boats, animals and scenes from daily life.
Kantha began as quilts, wraps and covers for children, and gifts for loved ones. The most ornate pieces, called nakshi kantha, tell stories in thread.
artist: Kantha is made by women, usually in spare hours at home, and is often a shared task between mothers, daughters and neighbours. The thread was traditionally pulled from the coloured borders of the old saris themselves.
Today women's collectives and social enterprises in Bengal pay for kantha work, which has given many rural women their own income.
Our approach: the stitcher's name and village should be on every piece.
place: Kantha is stitched across Bengal, in both West Bengal and Bangladesh. Birbhum, the district of Santiniketan, is a well-known centre in West Bengal.
Bengal's delta landscape, with its rivers, ponds and fish, is the world these designs are drawn from.

history.what: Quilted cloths in Bengal are mentioned in texts several centuries old.
Nakshi kantha was celebrated in Bengali literature, including the poet Jasimuddin's verse 'Nakshi Kanthar Math' (1929).
Self-help groups and cooperatives turned kantha into a livelihood.
It is found on saris, stoles and jackets, and in fashion.

future: Fair rates for stitchers and transparent pricing.
Keep upcycling at the heart of the craft, using real reused cloth.
Gather and archive heirloom kanthas and the stories attached to them.

name: Kashmiri Carpets
tagline: Hand-knotted wool and silk, woven from a coded pattern that weavers chant aloud.
facts: Local name: Kal baffi (hand-knotting)
The talim: a coded pattern, chanted or memorised
Materials: wool, silk, or a blend
Traditionally dated to the 15th century
art: A Kashmiri carpet is knotted by hand, one knot at a time, on a loom, usually in a weaver's home. Live History India says weavers use wool, silk or a blend, often dyed with natural colours: pomegranate peel for gold, indigo for blue and madder root for crimson.

The talim is the heart of the craft. It is a coded pattern on graph paper that tells where each colour goes, knot by knot. Live History India says weavers either chant it aloud or memorise it, so it works like a musical score for the hands.
Designs include the chinar leaf, the Tree of Life, Mughal-style medallions, pomegranate borders and charbagh garden layouts. A single carpet can take months, or even years, to finish.
artist: Many weavers learned from their parents and grandparents and still work on family looms, says Live History India. Women weavers also use the Senneh knot, an asymmetrical knot.
Government programmes such as One District One Product support artisan cooperatives. We did not find named master weavers in the sources we could open, so we name none.
The talim reader and the weavers work as a team, with one voice reading the pattern while the hands tie the knots.
place: Srinagar and the villages of Budgam are named as active weaving areas. Kashmir is the historic centre of the craft, says Wikipedia.
Kashmir lies on old routes to Persia and Central Asia, and its carpets drew on that world. Today they are found in museums and homes in cities such as London, Paris and Tokyo.

history.what: Live History India and Wikipedia both say the craft took root in this century under Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin, who brought weavers from Iran and Central Asia to train local people.
Wikipedia notes another account in which a Persian Sufi mystic's caravan of weavers brought the craft. Sources differ.
Live History India says that under the Mughals, including Akbar, Kashmiri carpets reached the courts of Agra and Delhi.
The same article says government initiatives revived the weaving clusters.
Wikipedia names mechanisation and powerlooms as a threat to the craft. Live History India notes renewed interest from slow fashion and sustainable luxury buyers.

future: Training: teach the talim to young weavers, since it is both a skill and an oral tradition.
Livelihood: pay fairly for the months a carpet takes, and support cooperatives.
Materials: keep natural dyeing alive and trace the wool and silk used.
Documentation: record talim codes, designs and the names of senior weavers.
Protection: help buyers tell hand-knotted carpets from machine-made ones. We saw reports of a Geographical Indication but did not confirm it from a page we read.

name: Kasuti Embroidery
tagline: Counted stitches, no knots, and temple towers sewn into silk by the women of north Karnataka.
facts: Form: counted-thread, knot-free hand embroidery
Four main stitches: gavanthi, murgi, negi, menthi
Classic piece: the black Chandrakali silk saree
Has a Geographical Indication (GI) tag; sources give 2006
art: Kasuti is a folk embroidery from Karnataka. The name is usually explained as kai (hand) and suti (cotton thread). It is worked by counting the threads of the cloth, so a design grows stitch by stitch without any drawn outline. Wikipedia and Outlook Traveller both note that craftswomen often work from memory, and that a pattern can take thousands of stitches. One article says more than 5,000.

Four stitches are named by most sources. Gavanthi is a double running stitch for straight and diagonal lines. Murgi is a zigzag. Negi is a running stitch used for spread-out designs. Menthi is a cross-stitch type that looks like fenugreek seeds and fills in motifs. The work is done without knots. Sources disagree on whether every stitch looks the same on both sides of the cloth. They agree it is meant to be neat on both faces.

The motifs come from daily life and from temples. Outlook Traveller lists lotuses, parrots, peacocks, swans, squirrels, bulls, elephants and deer. Gopurams (temple towers), chariots, palanquins and lamps also appear, along with patterns that resemble rangoli. Colours named include red, orange, yellow and purple.

The best known piece is the Chandrakali, a black silk saree with Kasuti on the border and pallu. Sources describe it as an important part of a bride's trousseau. Today Kasuti is also sewn on blouse pieces, tablecloths, bags, purses and other small items.
artist: Kasuti is traditionally women's work. Outlook Traveller says the designs reflect how the women see their world. The sources I read do not name individual embroiderers, so this entry does not either.

Wikipedia says that in the 17th century, women of the Mysore court were expected to learn 64 arts, and Kasuti was among them. It also dates the craft's history back to the Chalukya period. Outlook Traveller links it to the Chalukyas and later the Mysore dynasty. These are traditional accounts rather than dated records.

A government Kasuti centre was set up in Hubli to give rural women a place to learn and show their work. Wikipedia also says that a college course in Dharwad was closed, which it reads as a sign of weak support.
place: Kasuti belongs to the north Karnataka plateau, around Dharwad, Hubballi and Belagavi. Outlook Traveller also lists Bijapur, Miraj, Sangli and Jamkhandi among the places where it is found, which shows that the craft crosses the state border into Maharashtra.
This is cotton and silk country. The craft sits close to Ilkal, whose sarees often carry Kasuti on the pallu, and to the old weaving towns of the region.

A GI registration protects the name. Sources differ on the holder (Wikipedia names the Karnataka Handicrafts Development Corporation) and on the year. A Deccan Herald summary, which I could only see as a search snippet, gives 2006.

history.what: Wikipedia and Outlook Traveller link the embroidery to the Chalukya era. There is no dated record in the sources I read.
Wikipedia says women of the Mysore court were expected to master 64 arts, including Kasuti.
Kasuti sarees, above all the Chandrakali, become part of the bridal trousseau.
Kasuti receives a GI tag. Sources give 2006, though I could not confirm the year from the registry itself.
Government and trade bodies set up a centre in Hubli to promote the craft and display the work of rural women.
Wikipedia and Outlook Traveller describe the craft as under-supported and little known, though new products have helped it earn a living.

future: Training: keep Kasuti classes open in Dharwad, Hubballi and Belagavi, and teach counting-thread skill to young people.
Livelihood: pay fairly for the hours behind a single piece, and sell it as hand-counted work and not as machine imitation.
Materials: keep supplying good cotton, silk and thread so that the old Chandrakali saree can still be made.
Documentation: record the more than 700 designs that folk experts mention, with the names of the women who hold them.
Protection: use the GI tag to separate real hand Kasuti from printed copies.

name: Kerala Handloom (Kasavu)
tagline: Off-white cotton with a golden border, woven by hand in three Kerala villages.
facts: Fabric: undyed cotton with a kasavu (zari) border
Clusters: Balaramapuram, Kuthampully, Chendamangalam
GI: registered for all three
Garments: mundu, set-mundu, saree
art: Kerala's best-known handloom cloth is off-white cotton with a bright gold edge, called kasavu. Kasavu means the zari thread of the border. It is made into the mundu and set-mundu (two-piece dress) and into sarees.

Weavers use traditional throw-shuttle pit looms. A report on Balaramapuram says they do not use dobby or jacquard attachments for their designs. Borders may carry simple lines or motifs like Kathakali faces and Krishna, especially on Kuthampully sarees.
The pudava and kavani, a veshti and upper cloth with a pure zari border, remain a prized bridal gift. Kasavu clothing is worn widely at festivals such as Onam and Vishu and at weddings.

Each cluster has its own feel. Balaramapuram's cloth is fine cotton; Chendamangalam is known for soft, finer muslin-like kaithari weaves; Kuthampully for kasavu sarees and set-mundus. The handlooms are listed under Geographical Indications.
artist: Balaramapuram's weavers are mostly the Shaliar community, who speak Tamil and trace their descent from families brought from Tamil Nadu. Wikipedia says seven families were brought to weave for the royal family.

At Kuthampully, the Kerala Tourism page says the weavers' ancestors came from Mysore about 500 years ago to weave for the Cochin dynasty. The village's cooperative society was registered in 1972, and about 3,000 people work in the sector.
At Chendamangalam, reporting shows that most weavers are older women. In one society, only 24 of 648 registered weavers were actually weaving.
Our approach: profile weavers by name with their consent, and show the full chain from yarn to the finished border.
place: Balaramapuram lies near Thiruvananthapuram in southern Kerala. Kuthampully is in Thrissur district, in central Kerala. Chendamangalam is near Kochi, in Ernakulam district, about 40 km north of the city, near the Periyar river.
Kerala's hot, humid air suits breathable, lightly worked cotton. The traditional cloth is plain and rarely dyed, with gold only at the border.

Weaving here runs through cooperatives. Yarn, sizing space and sheds matter: Chendamangalam weavers say the open land needed to prepare warp is getting scarce, and heavy rain makes wooden looms hard to use.
Weaving is an income for families, but earnings are modest, as one report put it, about Rs 900 a week for a target length of cloth at Chendamangalam.

history.what: Weavers settle in Kerala under local rulers: Kuthampully's from Mysore under the Cochin dynasty, Balaramapuram's from Tamil Nadu under Travancore.
Under Maharaja Balarama Varma of Travancore and his minister Ummini Thampi, handloom weaving is introduced to Balaramapuram, which is named after the king.
Balaramapuram had about 5,100 looms in use, per Wikipedia.
The Kuthampully Handloom Industrial Co-operative Society is registered with 102 members.
Geographical Indication registrations for Balaramapuram, Kuthampully and Chendamangalam handlooms; sources give 2011 or 2012 for Chendamangalam.
Floods destroy looms and stock; Chendamangalam co-operatives estimate losses of about Rs 15 crore.
Power looms and falling prices leave many weavers with little work; some societies are shrinking sharply.

future: Fair, steady wages for weavers, with orders spread across the year, not only before Onam.
Strong authenticity labels so power-loom copies of kasavu are not sold as handloom.
Train young people with stipends and offer new design collaborations, with credit and pay to weavers.
Flood-safe sheds and insurance for looms, yarn and stock.
Preserve open warping spaces and build the planned handloom villages with weavers' input.
Natural-dye and ayurvastra experiments, led by weavers, for a premium market.

name: Khadda Weaving
tagline: Cotton woven on a pit loom, where the weaver's feet work below the floor.
facts: Loom: pit loom, called khaddi in some sources
Cloth: coarse cotton, plain or twill, in checks and stripes
Related product: khes, a cotton wrap and bedspread
Short entry: fewer sources found than for other forms
art: This entry is shorter than others because we found limited material under the name 'khadda'. The sources we could open describe the same family of Punjabi hand-woven cotton under the names khes and pit loom (khaddi, from khad, a pit).

Khes is a thick cotton cloth, woven from coarse yarn, used as a blanket, wrap or bedspread. One retailer's history page says it is made on household pit looms, in two narrow panels stitched together, in plain or twill weave with bold checks and stripes. Young INTACH describes khes as a thin hand-woven cotton blanket cloth.
The Village Square report on Balwaar village, Sangrur, says its weavers use the traditional kumbal pit loom, with a fly-shuttle loom to speed up work, and yarn from a spinning wheel.
artist: Young INTACH says village women traditionally wove khes for their wedding trousseau. The Balwaar project, which began a weaving pilot in 2017, now employs 22 local women trained in-house, according to Village Square. They make about one khes a day and earn Rs 10,000 to 50,000 a month depending on demand.
The same report says the studio is experimenting with natural dyes. We could not verify the names of other master weavers.
place: Young INTACH calls khes a common sight in rural Punjab. Amritsar, in contrast, is known for knotted galeecha carpets made by Kashmiri weavers who came in the early 19th century.
Balwaar in Sangrur is one working example of revival. We could not confirm other weaving clusters from pages we could open.

history.what: The page links khes to Mughal-era cotton weaving. Treat as an unconfirmed claim.
The same page says khes was most prominent then, across undivided Punjab.
The page says mill-made cloth and urban life caused a sharp decline.
The Balwaar weaving pilot began in Sangrur district (Village Square).
Designers and NGOs seek out old khes, and some weavers adapt its patterns for scarves and home goods.

future: Train more weavers on the pit loom and keep the skill in village hands.
Pay a steady wage, as Balwaar attempts, so weaving stays a real livelihood.
Use local cotton and natural dyes where possible.
Document patterns, loom parts and local names, including the term khadda itself.
Label hand-woven khes clearly against power-loom copies.

name: Khamti Weaving
tagline: Cloth of the Tai Khamti, from the sarong to the chief's silk coat.
facts: Community: Tai Khamti, mainly Buddhist
Listed in handloom GI sources as Tai Khamti Textile
Pattern types: geometric, animal and symbolic motifs (per one listing)
Evidence: thin; few detailed sources found
art: A government-linked handloom listing describes Tai Khamti textile as an age-old product with intricate, vibrant designs: geometric patterns, animal motifs and symbols with cultural and spiritual meaning. It also describes a silk coat worn by the Khamti chief.

Wikipedia's article on the Khamti describes dress rather than weaving. Men traditionally wear a full-sleeved cotton shirt and a multi-coloured sarong. Women wear a long-sleeved shirt, a deep-coloured sinh and a silk scarf, and married women add a plain black sarong and a green wrap.

General sources say Arunachal women commonly weave on back-strap looms, which are portable and easy to set up. I could not find a source that states the loom type, dyes or yarns for Khamti weaving specifically, so this entry does not.
artist: I did not find sources naming Khamti weavers. Durah writes that in Arunachal generally women weave on simple loin looms, but he does not single out the Khamti.
Durah notes that the Khamti also carve wood, including images of Buddha, animals and dolls. The Khamti are Theravada Buddhists and use their own script, Lik Tai, according to Wikipedia.
place: Wikipedia places the Khamti mainly in Namsai and Changlang districts of Arunachal Pradesh, with smaller numbers in Assam and in Myanmar. Namsai was part of Lohit district earlier, which is why older sources say Lohit. The 2011 census count for India was 16,944.
The same source says the Tai Khamti of the Tengapani basin descend from migrants who arrived in the 18th century from the Shan region of Hkamti Long, in present-day Myanmar.

history.what: Wikipedia says the Tengapani basin Khamti descend from migrants from Hkamti Long, in the Shan region of Myanmar.
The first printed book in the Lik Tai script appeared, per Wikipedia.
The census counted 16,944 Khamti in India.

Education and handloom listings name Tai Khamti textile among Arunachal textiles with a GI tag. A 2023 article lists it with Apatani, Monpa, Nyishi, Adi and Galo textiles but gives no date; check the official GI registry.

future: Training: record and teach Khamti weaving in community and monastery spaces, as with the script.
Livelihood: link weavers to the GI listing and to shops, with fair prices.
Materials: document yarns and dyes in use, including silk.
Documentation: this entry exists because little is written. A community study with Khamti weavers is the first need.
Protection: confirm GI details in the official registry and keep weavers' names on record.

name: Kharad Weaving
tagline: Bold flat-weave rugs of camel, goat and sheep hair, woven on a pit loom in Kutch.
facts: Form: flat-weave rugs and bags from Kachchh
Materials: camel, goat and sheep wool, with some cotton
Khamir says ten families wove it until the 1990s and only two remain
Products: kharad (floor spread), khurjani (camel bag), rasa (grain cover)
art: Kharad is a flat-weave carpet from Kachchh. Gaatha says the word is Sindhi for carpet. It grew from the needs of herding communities, and rugs, camel-back bags called khurjani and thick grain covers called rasa were made for daily life.

Wool came from camels, goats and sheep. Khamir says Maldhari and Rabari herders sheared the animals and hand-spinners made yarn. Dyes were plant-based, such as indigo, pomegranate rind, babool bark and lac, though many weavers now use chemical or vegetable dyes.

The yarn is coarse, so patterns are bold and geometric, inspired by the desert. Khamir says the rugs can last up to 100 years. Gaatha says later designs also show village life, farming, animals and the 2001 earthquake.
artist: Gaatha names Vankar (Marwada) weavers, descendants of Meghwal communities who came from Marwar in Rajasthan about 600 years ago. Khamir's own page names the Meghwal and Sodha Rajput. Aadyam says Rabari and Vankar artisans. Sources differ on who exactly weaves.

Khamir reports that ten families practised the craft until the 1990s and only two remain. They struggle to get regular orders. A weaver finishes only three to five pieces a month. We found no individual weavers named in the sources.
Khamir links artisans to buyers and exhibitions, and with Sahjeevan is rebuilding the chain from collecting camel hair to hand-spinning.
place: Gaatha names Kuran in north Kachchh, between the Great Rann and the Black Hills, as once a main centre. After the 2001 earthquake, artisans settled in Kukma, about 11 to 16 km from Bhuj, with help from government and NGOs.

The loom is a horizontal pit loom with two rods pegged to the ground. Gaatha says a mirror under the loom lets the weaver check the pattern. Khamir says nomadic looms could be set up and carried on animals.

history.what: Gaatha calls kharad an 800-year-old legacy. This is a general claim and we found no firm dates.
Khamir says kharad decorated palaces in Sindh and Gujarat, and kings and ministers were patrons.
Khamir says Partition cut off the Sindh market, which had bought many khurjani.
Khamir says ten families practised until then.
The earthquake destroys workshops and tools. Artisans resettle at Kukma.
Khamir and Sahjeevan rebuild a local camel-hair chain, and a Finnish organisation, Tikau, buys regularly.

future: Training: bring young people back to the loom while two families remain.
Livelihood: steady orders and buyers who pay for the work.
Materials: restore local hand-spinning of camel and goat hair, now lost in Kachchh.
Documentation: record patterns and loom practice from the surviving weavers.
Protection: teach buyers how long these rugs last, which Khamir says could widen the market.

name: Kosa Silk
tagline: Wild tasar silk, in gold, cream and brown, woven on handlooms in the Janjgir-Champa belt.
facts: Kosa is a local name for tasar silk
Silkworm: Antheraea mylitta, on arjun, saja and sal trees
GI application: Kosa Silk Saree and Fabric of Janjgir-Champa and Raigarh Region
GI status in 2011, according to Gaatha
art: Kosa is tasar silk from Chhattisgarh. It comes from the wild silkworm Antheraea mylitta, which feeds on trees such as arjun, saja and sal. The cloth is known for its sturdy texture and its natural shades of brown, cream and dull gold.

The GI application for Kosa silk describes two parts of the work. One is the rearing or collecting of cocoons and the reeling of yarn. The other is weaving. In the tribal areas of Raigarh, Sarguja and Bilaspur, silkworms are reared, and in Bastar cocoons are gathered in the forest. In Janjgir-Champa, reeling and weaving often go together in the home.

Weaving on handlooms follows preparation of warp and weft yarn. Gaatha lists three kinds of sari: phera, a plain body with a temple-shaped (kumbha) border; jala, with floral and geometric patterns made by the jala method; and khapa or patiya, with a ribbed pallu made using extra weft threads.

A plain Kosa sari can take three to five days, from yarn to weaving, depending on how many people work on it (Isha Foundation). Because the cocoon is scarce, Isha notes that yarn is sometimes mixed with cotton or polyester, so buyers should ask what they are getting.
artist: The weaving belt is associated with the Devangan and Koshta communities. The GI application tells a community story in which the goddess Durga blessed the Devangans to weave Kosa, and names Pankas, Julahas and Mehers among the groups involved. It is a story told in the application, not a documented history.
Wikipedia says Champa's merchants, largely of the Dewangan community, import tasar yarn from China and Korea and weave silk shirtings and saris. So today the sector uses both local and imported yarn.
The GI application was filed by the Champa Raigarh Hathkargha Kosa Samiti. It lists the weaver's family members as doing most of the preparation, with hired labour when needed.
place: Champa is a town on the Hasdeo river in Janjgir-Champa district, at about 22.05 N, 82.65 E. The GI application says the belt from Raigarh, with Janjgir-Champa at its centre, puts the most weight on Kosa silk. Korba, to the north, is also known for Kosa.
Champa's temples include Samleshwari Devi, and the town lives by weaving, trade, and some industry.

history.what: The GI application says the Kosa tradition is very old and links the word to the Sanskrit kauseya in the epics. These are claims in the application; we have not checked them against other sources.
The application records tariff protection for the industry.
The Central Silk Board is created.
The application records a government committee on the tasar industry (the Tasar Silk Committee).
Champa silk saris and fabrics receive GI status, according to Gaatha. We could not read the Registry entry, so please check the year.

future: Help weavers and cocoon gatherers keep the forest trees on which the wild silkworm depends.
Mark pure Kosa clearly, with labels that say how much is Kosa and how much is blended.
Fund training for young weavers in jala, patiya and phera designs.
Record the families and cooperatives behind each cloth, so buyers know who wove it.
Support weavers to sell directly, not only through traders.

name: Kota Doria
tagline: A cloth so light it is woven in tiny squares that let the air through.
facts: Form: handwoven cotton-silk cloth with a check called khat
Main centre: Kaithoon (Kaithun), about 15 km from Kota
GI status: sources give different years (1999, 2005)
Around 1,500 weavers, mostly women, per Textile Atlas
art: Kota Doria is a very light fabric woven with a grid of small squares called khat. Textile Atlas says small motifs are added with an extra weft, and zari is used mainly in borders and the pallu.
Wikipedia says cotton and silk were traditionally blended, roughly 20:80, and that pure silk versions are also woven. Early cloth was woven narrow for turbans and later wider for saris.
Textile Atlas says weavers at Kaithun still use the hand-throw shuttle on compact looms. Wikipedia says genuine pieces carry a GI mark woven into one corner.
artist: Textile Atlas says about 1,500 weavers work in Kaithun, mostly from the Ansari community and mostly women, many part-time from home. It names Badrun Nisha, who leads the Kota Women's Weavers Organisation, and master weaver Azgarbhai, who runs a workshop of 150 weavers.

The page notes that a single fine sari can take three months to weave. Power looms elsewhere imitate the cloth, and machine-made or printed cloth is sometimes sold as handloom, which weavers say hurts them.
place: Kaithun is a small village about 15 km from Kota. Wikipedia says weaving is centred there and in nearby villages. Most saris sold under the name are made on power looms in Surat and Varanasi, it says.

history.what: Wikipedia says that Jhala Zalim Singh is said to have brought weavers from Mysore to Kota, and the cloth was first called kota masuriya. Other sources name other patrons, and the story is unproven.
Early cloth was woven narrow for turbans, later wider for saris, per Wikipedia.
Textile Atlas gives 1999. Other sources I saw give 2005. The year is unsure.
Handloom weavers compete with power looms and say the craft gets little promotion, per Textile Atlas.

future: Pay weavers directly and fairly rather than through middlemen.
Use the GI mark to separate handloom from power-loom cloth.
Document the weaving and the Mysore link with proper research.
Support women weavers with yarn banks and training.
Reach buyers who value a three-month sari.

name: Kullu and Kinnauri Shawls
tagline: Woollen shawls with geometric borders, woven on home looms in the high valleys.
facts: Form: handwoven wool shawls with patterned ends
Kullu shawl: reported as the first Himachal product registered as a GI
Kinnauri shawl: GI registered October 2010 (Wikipedia)
About 15,000 weavers in the state in 2015 (Tribune)
art: In the cold Himalaya, people wove wool for warmth. Before patterned shawls, plain woven cloth called patti was worn. Shawls are made of sheep wool, yak wool, pashmina and other fibres.

A Kullu shawl typically has geometric designs at both ends, and some have floral designs across the whole piece. A design may use up to eight colours. Bright colours are traditional, though pastel versions exist.

A Kinnauri shawl is known for geometric designs, some with objects of religious importance. One source says its colours carry meanings: green for air, blue for ether, white for water, yellow for earth and red for fire. It is woven in two half-length pieces with matching designs, stitched together at the centre, and one shawl is said to take about 45 days. Commercial shawls are woven on frame looms; pit looms serve local use.
The geometric style is said to show Central Asian influence.
artist: The makers are weavers of Kullu and Kinnaur, working mostly on home looms. In 2015 officials counted about 15,000 weavers in the state, concentrated in Kullu, Kinnaur, Shimla, Mandi, Kangra and Chamba. Himbunkar is the state weavers' body.

Popular accounts say Kullu weaving came from Kinnaur and that skilled weavers from Bushahr settled in Kullu in the early 1940s, bringing patterned designs. These accounts mostly come from craft sellers and are not archival. The name Tanjenram Bhagat is given in some of them as the weaver of the first modern Kullu shawl in 1942. I could not confirm this in a scholarly source.
Weavers say imitations hurt them. In 2015 officials estimated that about 80 percent of shawls sold as Kullu or Kinnauri were made in Ludhiana factories.
place: The Kullu valley lies along the Beas river. Bhuntar, Naggar and Kullu town are well known for shawl weaving and sales. Kinnaur lies to the north-east along the Sutlej, with Rampur Bushahr to its west, where the two weaving traditions meet.
Winter is long and harsh in these valleys, which is why wool weaving became part of everyday life.

history.what: Plain woven patti cloth is worn against the cold.
Kinnauri weavers are said to have settled in the Kullu valley; this is not archival.
Bushahr weavers are said to bring patterned designs to Kullu.
Kullu shawl is reported as the first Himachal product registered as a Geographical Indication.
Kinnauri shawl is registered as a GI.
The state plans action against factory-made fakes and a GI awareness drive.

future: Training: apprenticeships so young weavers can learn pit-loom and frame-loom work.
Livelihood: sell through GI-marked outlets and government emporia, and run awareness drives for tourists.
Materials: secure supply of local wool and yak fibre and support natural dyeing.
Documentation: record patterns and their meanings from elder weavers.
Protection: enforce the GI against factory fakes.

name: Kunbi Saree
tagline: A red checked cotton sari, light enough for the paddy field.
facts: Worn traditionally by women of the Kunbi community
Checked cotton, red dominant, about six yards
Traditionally worn short, without a blouse
Revived since the early 2000s by designers and researchers
art: The Kunbi saree is a checked cotton sari of Goa. Isha's Save the Weave page calls it the oldest weave of the state. Red and its shades were traditionally the main colour. The cloth is sturdy, coarse and light, with a checked body, a shiny border at the bottom and no frills. It is woven on pit looms.

It is draped short, above the ankle, tied at the waist and knotted at the shoulder, traditionally with no pallu or blouse. This suited women working in the paddy fields. A Navhind Times column describes natural dyes made from rice starch, vinegar and iron ore, with red and blue noted. Isha's page says red was believed to come from a wild fruit called jafflinchi fala. Sources differ on the dye details.
The sari is also worn at ceremonies and religious events, and its checks are linked to natural forces, per Isha.
artist: The Kunbi are an indigenous community of Goa, known as early settlers and farm workers. Isha says the word combines kun (family) and bi (seed).

Local weavers had almost stopped weaving the cloth. Isha names Dr Rohit Phalgaonkar and Vinayak Khedekar among those working to revive it. The designer Wendell Rodricks showed a modern Kunbi collection with wider checks and softer colours; Isha dates it 2001, and other sources give 2010, so we leave the year open.
place: The Kunbi live in the villages of Goa, and the cloth belongs to farm life. A Navhind Times column mentions Big Foot at Loutolim, a cultural centre that held a textile exhibition in 2006 and honoured guests with Kunbi stoles.
Goa's legislators, including the Chief Minister, wore Kunbi stoles and caps at a monsoon session on National Handloom Day, the same column reports.

history.what: The Navhind Times column says Kunbi women wore the sari before the Portuguese arrived in the 16th century.
Isha says synthetic cloth and power looms moved much production to Maharashtra and cut the number of local weavers.
Designers and researchers began to revive the cloth, per Isha and the Navhind Times.
Modern versions appear in blues, greys and ivory. The Navhind column says Kunbi cloth would soon get a GI tag; we could not confirm that, so we do not state it.

future: Train new weavers on pit looms and pay them fairly while they learn.
Keep checked designs and natural dyeing recorded with the Kunbi families.
Make sure the Kunbi community, not only designers, earns from the revival.
Support yarn supply and dyeing materials within Goa.
Pursue legal protection of the weave, if the community wants it.

name: Kutch Embroidery
tagline: Mirrors and silk thread on cloth, where every stitch once told which community a woman belonged to.
facts: Form: hand embroidery with mirror work, from Kutch district
Communities: Rabari, Ahir, Meghwal, Sodha Rajput, Mutwa, Jat, Mochi and others
Named styles include Suf, Khaarek, Pakko, Neran and Rabari
Registered as a Geographical Indication; sources differ on the exact date
art: Kutch embroidery is not one craft but many. Wikipedia lists six main ethnic styles: Suf, Khaarek, Paako, Rabari, Garasia Jat and Mutava. Each community of Kutch stitched its own patterns on its own clothes, and the stitches and motifs showed who a woman was and where she came from.

A few styles show the range. Pakko is a tight chain stitch with symmetrical floral motifs, worked by Meghwal and Sodha Rajput women. Rabari work uses chain-stitch outlines and bold mirrors. Neran is made of tiny buttonhole stitches in geometric designs, with few mirrors. Ahir work is known for birds and flowers. Suf is built from counted triangles worked from the back of the cloth, with no outline drawn first. Khaarek covers the cloth in black-outlined squares filled with satin stitch.

The small mirrors, called abhla, are sewn on with thread to catch the light. Cotton, silk, wool and mashru cloth are all used. Common stitches named by sources include square chain, double buttonhole, pattern darning, running, satin and straight stitch.
Embroidery decorated daily and festive clothes and was part of a bride's trousseau. Live History India describes it as marking dowry, rites of passage, marital status and group identity.
artist: The makers are mostly women, who learned from their mothers and aunts. Wikipedia counts about 6,000 women engaged in the work. Sources name many communities, among them Rabari, Ahir, Meghwal, Sodha Rajput, Mutwa and Jat, and Mochi cobblers, who stitched with a hooked needle called aari.

Al Jazeera's 2018 report describes the Shrujan Trust, started by Chanda Shroff, who first visited Dhaneti in 1969. It began with 30 women from two communities and, by the report, reaches about 4,000 women in 120 villages. The report names artisans such as Mata Sariyaben, an Ahir artisan who heads the Dhaneti centre, and Fatmaben Musaabhai Mutwa, who trained about 22 young girls in stitches her mother and aunt knew.
The report adds that community elders once acted as chief design makers, assigning the designs. Shrujan later paid these designers to pass their skills to younger women.
place: Kutch is a large district of western Gujarat, with the Great Rann of salt desert to its north. It is dry, with open grassland and scattered villages. Sources note that none of the embroidering communities are native to the region. They came over the centuries from Sindh, Rajasthan and further west.

Bhuj is the main town and market. The Shrujan Trust's Living and Learning Design Centre in Bhuj opened in 2016 and documents 50 embroidery styles from 12 communities. Villages such as Dhaneti and Bhujodi appear in the reports as centres of artisan work.

history.what: Wikipedia dates the tradition to this period, a time of settlement in the region. Live History India says Mochi cobblers learned silk embroidery, traditionally from a Muslim ascetic of Sindh, and worked for the royal court of Bhuj. Sources differ on details.
The earliest style is called Mochi-Bharat or Aari-Bharat, after the hooked aari needle.
Communities who arrived from Sindh and Rajasthan brought their own stitch traditions, which developed separately.
Chanda Shroff first visits Dhaneti, beginning the documentation that led to the Shrujan Trust.
Kutch embroidery is registered as a Geographical Indication. Wikipedia lists March 2013 in one place and gives conflicting dates for the logo, so please check the GI registry.
The Living and Learning Design Centre opens in Bhuj.

future: Training: pass on stitches that only a few elders still know, through women artisans who teach younger girls, as Shrujan's master artisan model does.
Livelihood: fair, regular orders and home-based work so women can earn without leaving their villages.
Materials: support for good thread, cloth and mirrors, and design that keeps a community's own motifs.
Documentation: record each style under its community's name, with the artisans who stitched it.
Protection: use the GI registration so that machine copies are not sold as Kutch work.

name: Ladakhi Carpets
tagline: Wool floor coverings from a land of sheep, yaks and high winters.
facts: Fibre: sheep and yak wool
Tibetan knotted-pile carpets use a cut-loop knotting method
Nomad women weave floor coverings on looms
Evidence of weaving in Ladakh goes back to at least the 12th century
art: Our sources give only a partial picture of Ladakhi carpets, so this entry is short. Weaving in Ladakh uses mainly sheep and yak wool, with goat and yak hair. Sahapedia describes nomad women making floor coverings with a woven base of yak and sheep wool, with patterns added in acrylic yarn and the pile trimmed.

The wider Tibetan carpet tradition is better documented. The Rubin Museum describes two kinds. The planted-pile carpet (tsukden) is woven by nomads and farmers on horizontal frames and backstrap looms. The knotted-pile carpet (drumtse) is woven on a vertical loom by tying knots around a continuous warp thread. The museum calls this an archaic method, unlike pile weaving elsewhere. The general word for these carpets is den, meaning seat or cushion.
We did not find a source that dates a separate Ladakhi knotted-carpet tradition or describes its motifs, so we do not claim one.
artist: Weaving in Ladakh divides by community. Sahapedia says that in central and western villages men weave on portable foot looms, while among nomads women use backstrap looms and men use fixed-heddle looms. Women weave saddle coverings, tent walls and blankets of wool, and men weave tents and saddlebags from hair.

Dr Monisha Ahmed of the Ladakh Arts and Media Organisation studies these textiles. Courtauld's note on her talk says weaving is closely tied to birth and life, and that Moravian missionaries and government Handicraft Centres changed the tradition, as have Ladakhi fashion designers more recently. We found no named carpet weavers in sources we read.
place: Ladakh is high, cold and dry, and its herders keep sheep, yaks and goats. Wool is close to hand, and cloth and floor coverings are part of daily life. The Changpa nomads of Changthang weave on backstrap looms and get fine pashm through trade.
A wall painting at Saspol Cave shows a weaver at a foot loom, probably from the 12th to 14th century, and the earliest written mention of Ladakhi woollen cloth is from 1631, according to Sahapedia.

history.what: Clay spindle whorls from the Tibetan plateau suggest early spinning and weaving there.
The Rubin Museum says Tibetan pile weaving goes back at least to the early kings.
The Saspol Cave painting shows a foot-loom weaver.
The earliest written reference to Ladakhi woollen cloth, by the Portuguese priest Francisco de Azevedo.
Moravian missionaries and government Handicraft Centres changed Ladakhi weaving, per Courtauld.

future: Document knotted and planted-pile carpet making in Ladakh, with weavers' names and patterns, since little is written.
Support wool producers and spinners among the herding families.
Help weavers sell at fair prices through craft centres and cooperatives.
Teach young people to weave, as the next generation may not carry the craft.
Mark the difference between hand-made and machine-made carpets.

name: Lambani Embroidery
tagline: Mirrors, cowrie shells and 39 stitches, sewn by Lambani women of Sandur.
facts: Community: Lambani (Banjara, Lambada)
Sandur style called kasuthi kelsa
39 stitches; mirrors, cowries, coins and beads
GI tag; sources give 2008 or 2010
art: Lambani embroidery is made by women of the Lambani community, also called Banjara or Lambada. In Sandur, in Bellary district, the style is called kasuthi kelsa. It combines stitched designs, appliqué, patchwork and mirror work, and is decorated with cowrie shells, beads, coins and tassels.

30 Stades lists 39 stitch names for the Sandur style, among them bakkya, maki, vele, kilan, relo and gadri. Designs are geometric: triangles, squares, circles and diagonals, usually in contrasting thread.

The craft grew out of reuse. 30 Stades says women traditionally pulled threads from old sarees, sewed patches together and decorated them. The embroidery was part of the bridal trousseau and everyday dress, including a heavy skirt and blouse, and a chain of old coins called the rupaiya haar.

Today the same stitches are used on sarees, dupattas, kurtas, bags, cushion covers, wall hangings and belts. Colours have widened from reds, blacks, greens and yellows to include purple, pink and sky blue.
artist: The knowledge passes from mother to daughter. The News Minute reports that women learn while young and often embroider the dresses for a daughter's wedding.

In 1984 a local teacher, Mahalaxmi, began working with a small group of women in her courtyard in Sandur. With the help of M. Y. Ghorpade of the former Sandur royal family, the non-profit Sandur Kushala Kala Kendra (SKKK) was set up. The News Minute says it now employs over 400 women in about 15 villages, and 30 Stades says about 500 work with SKKK. The counts differ.

Shanta Bai Kallahalli began learning at 12, trained at SKKK at 18 and won a National Award in 2002 for a wall hanging, says 30 Stades. The News Minute also names award-winning artisans Gowri Bai and Shanti Bai, and designers Laila Tyabji, Laxmi Narayan and Roohi Azam who have worked with the group.
The News Minute says the work has given women income, confidence and mobility, and that embroidery pays less per day than sugarcane cutting. Some younger women prefer sarees to the traditional dress.
place: The Lambani are a semi-nomadic community, listed as a Scheduled Caste in Karnataka. 30 Stades says the 2011 census counted about 12.68 lakh Lambani people in the state. The News Minute gives a figure of about 1.1 million. Lambani homes are in settlements called thandas.

Sandur lies in Bellary district, in the dry north of the state. The News Minute says most unit workers live at Susheelanagar, and about 30 per cent of people from there go to cut sugarcane in other districts, which draws women away from the craft.

history.what: Accounts say the Lambani moved south from Rajasthan, some linking this to the Mughal army in the 16th century. Others tie it to the salt and grain trade. Some writers suggest a link to the Roma of Europe. Sources differ and these are contested accounts.
Mahalaxmi starts the Sandur work with a few women. SKKK is founded with M. Y. Ghorpade's backing.
30 Stades says the craft received UNESCO-CCI Seal of Excellence awards for South Asian handicrafts.
Shanta Bai Kallahalli wins a National Award.
Sandur Lambani embroidery receives a GI tag. The News Minute gives 2008 and 30 Stades gives 2010.
30 Stades says the work was shown at London Fashion Week.

future: Training: keep paid training for young women, as SKKK did when it trained 40 Scheduled Tribe women under a master craftsperson in 2020.
Livelihood: raise per-day earnings so that embroidery can compete with seasonal farm labour, and keep work available at home.
Materials: keep natural dyeing, hand-weaving and hand block printing alive.
Documentation: write down all 39 stitch names with the women who hold them.
Protection: give design credit to the women who stitch, and help them negotiate with designers.

name: Lepcha Weaving and Bamboo Craft
tagline: Striped back-strap cloth and a feathered bamboo hat, both made by the Lepcha, who call themselves Rong.
facts: Cloth is woven on a back-strap loom, with coloured warp stripes
The dumpra is a garment by day and a blanket by night
The sumok thyaktuk hat is made of bamboo and cane
Jordan Lepcha received the Padma Shri in 2024
art: The Lepcha weave on a narrow back-strap loom. Sikkim Tourism says the colourful stripes in the warp are the distinctive feature. Weavers once used nettle fibre and raw silk, and now use cotton and wool. Natural dyes came from roots, bark, fruit, leaves and vines.

Sahapedia describes the dumpra, a garment-blanket worn by Rong men as clothing by day and a blanket by night. Its named patterns include multicoloured stripes, a design from bamboo nodes, triangles based on the hat, arrow-tip V-shapes and one inspired by a spider's web.

Bamboo is central. Sahapedia says it is the core material for hats, baskets, utensils, musical instruments, traps and tools. It is harvested from April to June, when it is most pliable, shaved into thin strips and dyed with natural yellow and red. The thyaktuk hat has an inner base, a padding of dried leaves, and an outer web of cane and bamboo. Feathers are attached at the front, the most prized being a racket-tailed drongo's tail.
There are several hat styles. The sumok thyaktuk is the most elaborate, linked to war and festivals. The pabri is simpler and cheaper. The na-rek thyaktuk is conical and worn by dancers.
artist: Women have traditionally woven for their households and communities. Sikkim's craft department says Lepcha women have woven since ancient times, while the men hunted and fished.

Hat making is now limited to a small number of skilled weavers, says Sahapedia. One is Jordan Lepcha of Lower Lingdong, Mangan district, selected for the Padma Shri in 2024 according to The Week. He makes the sumok thyaktuk, which takes about six weeks and costs Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000. He has taught over 150 young people, many of whom now earn a living from bamboo crafts. He supports a GI tag, and the Sikkim government has started the registration process, the report says.
Sahapedia records a Rong saying: till bamboo exists, so will the Rongs.
place: The Lepcha are an indigenous people of Sikkim, living in the Dzongu valley in the foothills of Kanchenjunga, according to Sikkim Tourism. Sahapedia also mentions Kalimpong and Darjeeling, where traditional weaving declined and young artisans are working to revive it.
The Directorate of Handicrafts and Handloom in Gangtok is where Sahapedia photographed the loom, and government cottage industries now produce much of the dumpra.

history.what: Rong oral histories say the god of music and dance, Narok Rum, gave the Rong a feathered hat as a reward for dancing and singing.
Hunter's Statistical Account of Bengal describes the sumok, according to Sahapedia.
The sumok thyaktuk was popular, worn by Lepcha home guards.
Village weaving gave way to government-funded cottage industries in Sikkim, and weaving declined in Kalimpong and Darjeeling.
Jordan Lepcha was selected for the Padma Shri for his work preserving the craft.

future: Training: more master-apprentice teaching, building on Jordan Lepcha's 150 trainees.
Livelihood: pay fair prices for six-week hats and woven cloth, and sell directly to buyers.
Materials: protect bamboo and cane groves and revive nettle fibre.
Documentation: record the Rong names for patterns and hat parts.
Protection: follow the GI registration process the report mentions, and keep ceremonial use of the hats alive.

name: Manipuri Handloom
tagline: Cloth woven by Meitei women, sold in a market run only by women.
facts: Medium: cotton and silk
Technique: loin-loom and frame-loom weaving
Garments: phanek, moirang phee
art: Manipuri handloom has strong geometric borders and bright stripes. The phanek is a wrap-around skirt worn by Meitei women, and Moirang phee is a traditional cloth with distinctive patterns.
Textiles also mark ritual and festival occasions, and each community of Manipur has its own weaving styles.
artist: Weaving is traditionally done by women, and the craft is part of home life across the valley.
Imphal's Ima Keithel ('Mothers' Market') is a large market run only by women and is one of the best-known places to buy their cloth.
Our approach: highlight the women's stories and their economic role.
place: Imphal sits in a valley ringed by hills, beside Loktak Lake. The valley's farming and festivals provide the context for the cloth.
Manipur's many communities, including Meitei, Naga and Kuki, each have distinctive weaving.

history.what: Textiles are mentioned in Manipur's chronicles and ritual traditions.
The women's market is said to be centuries old and continues today.
Weavers combine traditional patterns with modern garments.

future: Document patterns of every community's weaving.
Fair markets that support women's cooperatives.
Keep the loom in schools and homes.
