name: Mata ni Pachedi
tagline: A shrine in cloth, made by a community the temple would not admit.
facts: Medium: cotton cloth
Technique: hand-painted and block-printed
Colours: natural red and black from madder and iron
art: Mata ni Pachedi means 'behind the Mother Goddess'. It is a cloth shrine, hung as a canopy and backdrop for a Mother Goddess image. It is painted in red and black on white cotton.
The central panel shows the goddess, surrounded by attendants, animals and devotees. Cloth was traditionally washed in the river, where its natural dyes set.
artist: The craft is made by the Vaghri community, historically denied entry to some temples. They created their own shrines in cloth and worship at them.
A few families in Ahmedabad keep the tradition. Many of the artists are also devotees; the work is both livelihood and worship.
Our approach: let the community decide how, and what, to share.
place: Ahmedabad on the Sabarmati river was a major textile city. Pachedi workshops sit on its edge, near riverside spaces once used to wash cloth.
Gujarat's long tradition of block-printing and natural-dye work forms the craft's backdrop.

history.what: The craft is believed to be several centuries old and tied to Mother Goddess worship.
Industrial printing and river pollution cut the supply of washing space and clean water.
A few families work on both ritual and decorative commissions.

future: Clean river access for dyeing and washing.
Support for the few remaining families to train apprentices.
Respect: separate sacred shrine-making from commercial products.

name: Murshidabad Silk
tagline: Mulberry silk from the old Nawabs' capital, once traded to half the world.
facts: Made from mulberry silk (Bombyx mori)
Kasimbazar trading post set up in 1658, says Wikipedia
GI applied for in 2023; outcome not confirmed here
Sericulture farmers fell from 38,040 (2002) to 14,593 (2012)
art: Murshidabad silk is fine, light and easy to drape. Wikipedia says its best-known saris are Baluchari and Gorood. Isha's Save the Weave page says the cream-coloured base takes dye well, giving deep maroons, reds and purples.

Weavers pattern the cloth with a supplementary weft, as Isha describes it. The pallav carries the picture. It has shown social life, steam engines, European rulers and hookahs, with no fixed design code.
Isha notes that spinning the yarn and weaving the cloth under one roof can still be seen in Murshidabad. A sari takes about four days, and weavers earn roughly Rs 100 a day, it says.
artist: The sources I read name no living weavers. They describe the weavers as heirs of the artisans who moved with the Nawab, with many younger people leaving.
Wikipedia lists causes of decline: degraded silkworm strains, mulberry loss to drought and floods, trouble getting bank loans and better-paid city jobs.
place: Murshidabad district lies on the Bhagirathi. Wikipedia calls it West Bengal's second-largest and India's third-largest silk-producing district. Cossimbazar, about 9 km from Murshidabad town, was a silk centre.
The textile ministry lists Murshidabad as one of six mega handloom clusters, according to Isha.

history.what: Production is said to have begun, per Wikipedia. Sources do not agree on early dates.
The East India Company sets up a trading post at Kasimbazar. Dutch, Portuguese and French traders follow.
Nawab Murshid Quli Khan moves the capital and his weavers move with him.
Tipu Sultan reportedly sends an expert to learn silk methods (Wikipedia).
Factories close because of losses.
The Bengal famine is a major setback.
Sericulture farmers fall from 38,040 to 14,593; weavers from 25,778 to 15,160.
WBNUJS applies for a GI tag. I could not confirm the result.

future: Training: restore good silkworm rearing and new pattern work.
Livelihood: bank credit and direct markets, which Isha says weavers lack.
Materials: better cocoon quality and mulberry supply.
Documentation: record old pictorial designs.
Protection: pursue and check the GI application.

name: Mysore Silk
tagline: Pure silk and gold-silver zari from a royal factory founded in 1912, still woven in Mysuru.
facts: Type: mulberry silk, with a Geographical Indication tag
Factory founded 1912 by Krishnaraja Wodeyar
Now run by Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation (KSIC)
Cocoons mainly from Ramanagara district
art: Mysore silk is a mulberry silk from Mysuru. It is best known as the sari, woven with a zari border. Wikipedia reports that the zari contains 65 percent pure silver and 0.65 percent gold. This figure is from a 2019 newspaper report, so check it with KSIC before quoting.

Wikipedia describes the process. Cocoons are bought, mainly from Ramanagara, and boiled into thread at a raw silk plant in T. Narasipura. The thread is then woven into saris and other products at the factory in Mysuru.
artist: Wikipedia does not name individual weavers. The craft today is tied to the Mysore silk factory, run by KSIC since 1980, so its makers are mostly factory weavers.
I could not find reliable named artisans, so none are named.
place: Mysuru in southern Karnataka is the home of the weaving factory. Ramanagara district supplies cocoons, and the raw silk plant is at T. Narasipura.
Wikipedia says Karnataka produces about 9,000 metric tons of mulberry silk, nearly 45 percent of India's total.

history.what: The regional silk industry declines after the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire, per Wikipedia.
The industry is revived under Tipu Sultan, per Wikipedia. The details of his role come from weaker sources and vary.
Maharaja Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar founds the Mysore silk factory.
The Mysore State Sericulture Department runs the factory.
The Karnataka government hands it to KSIC.
Mysore silk appears in the Geographical Indications Journal as a GI product.

future: Train young weavers and pay them fairly, since the factory depends on a small skilled workforce.
Test and publish zari content, so buyers can trust the label.
Support sericulture farmers in Ramanagara with fair cocoon prices.
Record old designs and loom methods before they are lost.
Guard the GI mark against copies sold as Mysore silk.

name: Naga Shawl Weaving
tagline: Each Naga tribe has its own colours and motifs, woven by women on the backstrap loom.
facts: Woven mainly by women on the loin (backstrap) loom
Each tribe has its own colour and motif code
Chakhesang shawls received a GI tag in 2017, per Rural India Online
Examples: Ao Tsungkotepsu, Lotha Sutam, Angami and Chakhesang Lohe
art: A Naga shawl tells who wears it. Live History India says shawls and sarongs show tribal identity and social status, and each Naga tribe has its own colour and motif code. Designs use straight lines, squares, bands and stripes, mostly in red, white, black and blue.

Motifs carry meaning. The mithun, a large bovine, appears on shawls of those who gave a feast of merit. Spears, the dao (machete), the tiger and the hornbill stand for strength and valour. The same article lists shawls by tribe: the Ao Tsungkotepsu, a warrior shawl with a dark base, white middle bands and black and red bands; the Lotha Sutam, white with dark blue stripes; the Phom Henyu, red; and the Sangtam Supong, black with grey bands.

The Lohe is a shawl of the Angami and Chakhesang. Wikipedia describes it as black with broad red and green bands, the green once yellow, traditionally worn by men, and often woven in narrow strips stitched together. Sources I read differ on whether it is worn by men or women, so I follow Wikipedia.

The main loom is the loin, or backstrap, loom. The warp is stretched between bamboo sticks, with one end tied to the weaver's back and the other to a wall or door. Some tribes also use pit and fly-shuttle looms. Cotton was traditional. Dyes came from forest plants such as Assam indigo for blue, but chemical dyes are common now.
artist: Weaving is traditionally women's work. Girls start young. According to Live History India, Lotha women were not thought ready for marriage until they could weave a man's loincloth. Ao folklore credits a woman named Longkongla with starting weaving, and the article presents this as legend.

Rural India Online follows Kuzhami Chakhesang weavers in Pfutsero, Phek district. Kekuwe-u estimates about 11 per cent of its 266 households weave. Vehusulu is a fourth-generation weaver. The women say weaving brings about Rs 1,000 to 1,500 a week against Rs 500 to 600 for daily labour, but that it is hard on the back, fits around farm work, and gets little government help. These are the weavers' own estimates.
Women also weave mekhala sarongs for their families.
place: Nagaland has many tribes, each with its own region and weaving tradition. Pfutsero, in Phek district, is a Chakhesang village. The Ao live mainly in Mokokchung district and the Konyak in Mon.
Weavers buy yarn in bulk in the November to December peak season. Cotton and wool, including imported yarn, are now more common than traditional plant fibres such as stinging nettle.

history.what: Live History India says the early history of the Nagas is lost, and no record shows when weaving began.
Mithun-head shawls are worn by those who performed a feast of merit, per Live History India.
Warrior culture has faded. Colours such as pink and green on black now appear, and some designs show church bells and holly.
Chakhesang shawls receive a GI tag, per Rural India Online.
Weavers sell to shops and online platforms, while competing with machine-made cloth.

future: Training: girls learn by watching mothers and grandmothers. Short courses on design and costing can add to this.
Livelihood: weavers say pay is low and buyers ask for discounts. Fair price tags and direct sales could help.
Materials: yarn is mostly bought. Reviving natural dyes and fibres would link the cloth back to its roots.
Documentation: Rural India Online notes most weavers interviewed did not know the names or meanings of motifs. Recording them from elders would help.
Protection: the GI tag for Chakhesang shawls needs enforcement against machine-made copies.

name: Paithani Sarees
tagline: A silk sari whose peacock pallu is woven by hand, one small motif at a time.
facts: Form: handloom silk sari with zari, woven in six or nine yards
Main motifs: peacock (mor), lotus (kamal), vine (asawali), parrot (tota)
Centres: Paithan and Yeola
A fully handwoven sari takes at least three months, Sahapedia reports
art: A Paithani is a handloom silk sari with zari, thread of gold or silver. It is traditionally woven in six or nine-yard lengths. Sahapedia names its main parts as the body, the zari border (kath) and the pallu (padar), the end piece that hangs over the shoulder.

The pallu is woven first, with zari weft over silk warp, and it can take from two weeks to two months. The body carries small woven dots and motifs called buttis, 200 to 300 on one sari according to Sahapedia. Wikipedia describes the weave as a plain weave with weft-figured designs worked on tapestry principles, including the interlocking kadiyal method.

The motifs come from nature. Sahapedia lists the peacock (mor), the bangdi mor or bangle peacock, the lotus (kamal), the vine (asawali), the parrot (tota) and the sunflower. It calls the bangdi mor the hardest motif to weave. Colour is played with too: weaving a warp of one colour with a weft of another gives a shot-silk glow called dhoop chaon.

Time is the real cost. Sahapedia reports that a weaver averages about two inches of pallu or five to six inches of body a day, so a fully handwoven sari takes at least three months. Wikipedia cites longer figures for very fine designs, and sources differ.
artist: Sahapedia names the communities who have woven Paithani as the Sali, Koshti and Momin. Other families supplied the dyeing (Bhavsar), the gold and silver work (Sonar) and the zari. Master weavers once kept four to eight looms and trained apprentices who began at 12 or 14 and spent two to four years learning before weaving a full sari.

That chain has thinned. Sahapedia says that in Paithan only three or four families can trace an unbroken weaving line of four or five generations, and that zari making and silk preparation have almost vanished from the town. Today many weavers there learned in workshops run under a Government of Maharashtra initiative. The same article says the Paithani Kala Kendra has trained about 200 women, and that some centres are moving weaving from a mostly male trade to a mostly female one.
Our approach: name the weavers and the families who still hold the full chain of skills, and show the hours inside one pallu.
place: Paithan lies on the Godavari in the Marathwada region. It was the ancient Pratishthana. Sahapedia describes it as a trade and textile town from the 2nd century BCE whose silks and cottons were traded with Rome.

Yeola, in Nashik district, is the other centre and today the larger one. Sources agree that weavers moved there from Paithan, but they give different reasons and dates. Wikipedia says the Peshwas moved weavers to Yeola in the 17th century, while Sahapedia mentions a 12th-century move after an invasion by Siddharaja Solanki of Gujarat.

Sahapedia notes that the Yeola sari is woven on a faster kadhiyal loom and is cheaper, while the Paithan sari is the GI-protected product. Check the label: Wikipedia and Sahapedia both report that power-loom copies are widely sold as Paithani.

history.what: Paithan, then Pratishthana, is described by Sahapedia as a textile trade town whose silks and cottons were exchanged for Roman goods. Writers often link Paithani to the Satavahana period, but the sari as we know it cannot be traced that far back.
Sahapedia says the Paithani traces its origin to brocades made in Paithan under the Yadavas.
Weavers moved from Paithan to Yeola. Accounts differ on when and why: Sahapedia mentions a 12th-century invasion, Wikipedia a 17th-century Peshwa decision.
Sahapedia says the craft flourished, with patrons that included Aurangzeb, the Marathas, the Peshwas and the Nizams.
The craft is described as being at its peak.
A slow decline followed, according to Sahapedia.
The craft was revived with state support.
Wikipedia reports a GI tag for Paithani; the entry notes the claim lacks a citation. Sahapedia and other sources also report it as GI protected.

future: Training: expand apprenticeships so that young weavers learn the full chain, from warp preparation to the bangdi mor, and pay them while they learn.
Livelihood: protect weavers from power-loom copies sold as handloom, with clear GI, Silkmark and Handloom Mark labels at every shop.
Materials: bring back local zari and silk preparation, which Sahapedia says have almost disappeared in Paithan.
Documentation: record the pallu and butti patterns and the names of the old weaving families before the last masters retire.
Protection: educate buyers on how to tell handloom from power loom, and publish prices that reflect months of work.

name: Panipat Khes Weaving
tagline: A thick cotton bedspread woven in checks, now rare even in its home town.
facts: Form: coarse handwoven cotton blanket cloth
Patterns: plain, checks and diamonds
Used as bedding, wrap and part of a bride's trousseau
Now rare; sources disagree on who still weaves it
art: Khes is a thick cotton cloth used for blankets and winter wraps in the northern subcontinent. Wikipedia says it is generally handwoven with coarse cotton yarns, and that it can be plain or geometric, with checks and diamonds. Named types include patpatti (white and red checks), tukridaar (white and blue checks) and dabba khes with squares of dyed yarn.

A writer for the Museum of Material Memory describes khes as a sturdy bedspread that served as bedding, a shawl, a floor mat and back support. She groups it into three kinds by weave: saada, gumti and majnu. Majnu is the most complex, using a double-cloth weave, and gives a bold graphic pattern.

Panipat is listed by Wikipedia as an Indian production area for khes, with no further detail. The same museum writer went to Panipat to find majnu khes, which online articles claimed was still made there. She found no trace of it, and nobody she met knew the name. I could not read other accounts that describe weavers there.
artist: In the Punjab region, khes was woven by village weavers, called Julaha, for sale, and women also wove it at home, says the Museum of Material Memory. Wikipedia adds that khes was often part of a bride's trousseau.

ETV Bharat reports that Khemraj Sundariyal, an 84-year-old handloom and tapestry weaver settled in Panipat since 1975, received the Padma Shri in the 2026 awards. The report calls his craft handloom weaving and tapestry. It does not say that he weaves khes, so he should not be named as a khes weaver without a source.
place: Panipat is in Haryana, about 95 km north of Delhi on NH-44, and is known as a textile city. Wikipedia lists wool and cotton milling among its industries and says it is called the city of weavers. It is also known for the three battles of Panipat in 1526, 1556 and 1761.

The Museum of Material Memory says the khes that survives in India often came with families who migrated at Partition in 1947, and that majnu khes is still made in Pakistan, at Multan and Bhera, but on power looms.

history.what: Wikipedia notes that the region was known for coarse cotton textiles, citing old gazetteers.
At Partition, many weavers of western Punjab moved and the exchange of the craft across the border stopped, says the Museum of Material Memory.
Khemraj Sundariyal settles in Panipat as a handloom weaver, according to ETV Bharat.
Other accounts I could not open say hundreds of looms once wove khes in Panipat and that powerlooms led to its decline. I could not confirm these figures.
Khemraj Sundariyal receives the Padma Shri, per ETV Bharat.

future: Documentation: record the surviving weavers and their looms, and the weave structure of each khes type, before it is lost.
Training: teach the double-cloth weave to young weavers in Panipat.
Livelihood: link weavers to buyers who value handwoven bedspreads over powerloom copies.
Research: find out through field surveys whether khes is still woven in Panipat today, since sources conflict.

name: Patola of Patan
tagline: Silk saris whose threads are dyed before weaving, so the pattern appears on both sides.
facts: Form: double-ikat silk, tied and dyed in both warp and weft
One sari takes about six months, with dyeing alone taking months
Associated with the Salvi family of Patan
Weavers' arrival in Patan is told in legend, with sources differing on date
art: Patola is a double-ikat silk. Both the warp and weft threads are tied and dyed to the pattern before weaving. The design shows only when the weaver lines the two sets of threads up exactly. A Better India feature describes the finished sari as reversible.
The Salvi loom is a hand-operated harness loom of rosewood and bamboo. Gaatha explains that the family name Salvi comes from sal, loom, and vi, a rosewood implement used on it.

Patola designs are geometric, floral and figurative, with sharp outlines. Gaatha notes that similar designs appear in the carved panels of the 11th-century Rani-ki-Vav step well in Patan. Red and green are described there as auspicious and protective colours.

The Better India says the Salvi family uses natural dyes such as indigo, turmeric, madder root, pomegranate skin and marigold, and pure mulberry silk. It reports six months for a six-yard sari, with three to four months for dyeing, and prices from about Rs 1 lakh.
artist: The Salvi family of Patan is the best-known keeper of the craft. The Better India says they are reportedly the only family in Patan weaving patola entirely with natural dyes. A 2020 report quotes Rahul Salvi calling his family the only one doing this, so this is the family's own claim and other families have also been reported.

Rahul Salvi is described as a master weaver who left an architecture career to join the family trade. Reports differ on when. The family opened the Patan Patola Heritage museum in 2014, with live loom demonstrations and textiles from other ikat traditions for comparison.
The craft is hard on the family. Dyeing and tying take months, and only a few families keep double ikat alive.
place: Patan lies in north Gujarat and was the capital of Gujarat until 1411, according to Gaatha. The Salvi weavers lived in Salvivad in the old town, where the long straight streets are said to have been laid out so warp threads could be stretched along them.
Patan is reached from Ahmedabad (about 125 km) by road, or via Mehsana, about an hour away. The Gujarat Tourism page lists the museum's hours as 10 am to 6 pm.

history.what: Sources disagree. Gaatha says patola may go back to the 7th century. The Better India cites the Narasimha Purana for early mentions in south India.
Legend says King Kumarpal of the Solanki dynasty brought about 700 weaver families from Jalna to Patan. Dates and reasons vary by source, so treat the story as tradition.
Gaatha says patola was exported to Indonesia and Malaysia, where it was valued as a sign of rank.
The Better India says one patola then cost Rs 120.
The Better India says the Salvi family used chemical dyes for a time and later returned to natural ones.
The Salvi family opens the Patan Patola Heritage museum.

future: Training: bring new weavers into the family tradition and open workshops for outsiders.
Livelihood: fair prices for work that takes months, and honest labelling of what is true double ikat.
Materials: keep access to natural dyes and good mulberry silk.
Documentation: record the tying and dyeing steps and the patterns with the people who know them.
Protection: sources conflict on GI status, so confirm it in the GI registry before relying on it.

name: Phulkari
tagline: Flowers in silk floss, stitched on the back of rough cotton, one bride's lifetime at a time.
facts: Form: darn-stitch embroidery in untwisted silk floss on hand-woven cotton
Name means 'flower work'; bagh means 'garden'
GI status granted (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan); sources give 2010 or 2011
Traditionally made by women for dowry and family use
art: Phulkari is the folk embroidery of Punjab. The name means flower work, though the designs also use geometric shapes. Women worked darn stitches on the reverse of coarse, hand-woven cotton cloth called khaddar, using untwisted silk floss known as pat. They usually worked without tracing the design or following a pattern book.

Not all phulkari is the same. In the narrow sense, a phulkari is a lightly embroidered shawl where the base cloth still shows. A bagh, meaning garden, is covered almost completely with stitches so the cloth is hidden. Wikipedia lists variants such as ghungat bagh, vari da bagh and bawan bagh. Other types include the chope, a bridal piece embroidered on both sides, and the sainchi, the one style where outlines are drawn in ink and which shows village life.

Red and its shades were favoured as auspicious. Backgrounds were often madder brown, rust or indigo. The Young INTACH craft map for Punjab also names phulkari and bagh as embroidered odhnis and chaddars, and notes khaddar as the base cloth.

Phulkari was part of a bride's dowry. Wikipedia says pieces were often made over many years, sometimes starting when a girl was born, and were worn at weddings and festivals and kept as heirlooms rather than sold.
artist: Phulkari was traditionally a household art of Punjabi women. It was made for the family, not for the market, and skill was passed from mother to daughter.

The craft declined by the 1950s, and fewer women now know the older techniques. Wikipedia notes that many present-day embroiderers use tracing blocks, that machine-made imitations on synthetic cloth are widespread, and that hand embroidery is slow and hard on the eyes and pays little.

After Partition in 1947, organisations encouraged women to embroider phulkari for income. NGOs, cooperatives and government programmes now offer training and sales, and designers use phulkari on clothes and accessories. This entry does not name individual embroiders because we did not find a source we could open that does so.
place: Phulkari belongs to the Punjab region, and is shared by Indian Punjab, Haryana and Pakistan. The Geographical Indication registration covers Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.
Khaddar, the cotton base cloth, comes from village weaving. In this way phulkari links two crafts: the weaving of the cloth and the embroidery over it.

history.what: Some writers see an earlier form of this reverse-side embroidery in Bana's Harshacharita. This is an interpretation, not a settled fact.
Wikipedia says the earliest known use of the word phulkari is in Waris Shah's Heer Ranjha.
Scholars disagree. One theory links the craft to migrants from Central Asia, another to Iran's gulkari. Pal (1960) argues phulkari is distinct and Punjabi.
Export demand began to change designs, and writers disagree about the effect.
Partition disrupted the craft. Groups then encouraged women to embroider for income.
The craft is said to have declined by this time.
Phulkari received a Geographical Indication. Wikipedia gives 2011; other sources give 21 October 2010, so we say 2010 or 2011.

future: Support training for young women, with fair piece rates so the work is worth their time.
Pay hand embroiderers more than machine copies earn, and label hand work clearly under the GI.
Keep supplying hand-woven khaddar and good thread, so the base cloth survives too.
Record the older designs (bagh, chope, sainchi) and the women who still know them, with photographs and oral histories.
Protect the GI name against machine-made products sold as phulkari.

name: Pipli Applique
tagline: Cut-cloth canopies and umbrellas made for Lord Jagannath's chariots.
facts: Also called Chandua
Techniques: appliqué and reverse appliqué
Made in Pipili, about 40 km from Puri
Holds a Geographical Indication
art: Pipli applique, also called Chandua, is a craft of stitching shapes cut from coloured cloth onto a base cloth. In plain appliqué a shape is sewn on top. In reverse appliqué a shape is cut out of the top layer to show the layer beneath.

Flat motifs are cut, laid out in a set plan and fixed with straight, blind, satin or buttonhole stitches. Some pieces add mirror work. Gaatha adds that a distinctive Odisha style folds the cloth into triangles to give a three-dimensional effect.

Common designs are elephants, parrots, peacocks, ducks, lotus, jasmine, trees, the sun, the half moon and Rahu. The traditional items are the chhati (umbrella), tarasa (a heart-shaped canopy piece), chandua (an umbrella-shaped canopy) and jhalar (a frill).

The best known work is on the cloth covers of the three Ratha Yatra chariots at Puri. Gaatha gives each a fixed colour scheme: green and red for Balabhadra, black and red for Subhadra, and yellow and red for Jagannath.
artist: Gaatha says the craft is traditionally practised by the Darji community of tailors, who regard the work as seva, or service to the Lord. The community has a chief and holds annual meetings.
Today the same hands also make bags, cushion covers, bed sheets and wall hangings. Base cloth and thread are bought from outside the town, as Gaatha notes cloth from Kolkata and thread from Surat.
We could not find individual artisans named in the sources we read, so none are named here.
place: Pipili is a small town in Puri district, about 40 km from Puri. Wikipedia says its economy depends largely on handicrafts, with appliqué the main source of income.
Gaatha says the village was set up by a local king to house craftsmen who made appliqué umbrellas and canopies for the Jagannath Yatra.

history.what: Wikipedia dates the craft's origin to the 12th century, tied to the worship of Lord Jagannath.
Appliqué canopies, umbrellas and lanterns were made for the annual Ratha Jatra under the Gajapati kings.

Gaatha says the craft reached its peak under royal and noble patronage and moved from temple art into household and decorative goods. It gives the 11th century for this peak, while Wikipedia gives the 12th century for the origin. Sources differ.
Pipili received a Guinness World Records entry for the largest thematic appliqué work, a 54-metre piece on India's freedom struggle, according to Wikipedia.
The Government of India granted the craft a Geographical Indication.

future: Livelihood: steady orders beyond the festival season, through fair trade shops, wholesale and online sales.
Training: teach cutting, folding and stitching to young people in Pipili with master tailors.
Materials: keep good quality cloth and colourfast dyes within reach of small workshops.
Documentation: record designs, stitch names and the colour rules for the chariot covers.
Protection: use the GI so that machine-made copies are not sold as Pipili work.

name: Pochampally Ikat
tagline: Threads tied and dyed before they are woven, so the pattern appears on the loom.
facts: Form: double ikat, with warp and weft resist-dyed before weaving
Local names: Paagadu Bandhu and Chitki
Fibres: cotton, silk and a silk-cotton blend called sico
GI registered; sources give 2004 or 2005
art: Pochampally ikat is a woven cloth in which the pattern is made in the thread, not on the cloth. Before weaving, bundles of yarn are tied tightly in places so that dye cannot reach them. The yarn is then dyed, sometimes in several colour stages, and the ties are opened. The tied parts keep their old colour. When the yarn is woven, the pattern appears.

Pochampally is described as a double ikat tradition. This means the warp and the weft are both resist-dyed, and the two sets of threads must line up exactly on the loom. One feature article says the designs are symmetrical and geometric, with softly blurred edges, and that planning a design can take weeks.

The cloth can be cotton, silk or sico, a silk-cotton blend. Locally the dyeing method is called Paagadu Bandhu, and the cloth is also called Chitki. Sarees are the best-known product, but the same weaving is used for dress material and home furnishing.

Sources do not agree on the numbers. One feature says about 10,000 families in nearly 40 villages and about 5,000 pit looms across two clusters. Another page says a cluster of 80 villages. Please treat the figures as rough.
artist: Ikat work is shared among many hands. Yarn is wound, tied, dyed, washed, set up on the loom and woven, and each step has its own skilled worker. Feature writing says cooperatives, private firms and master weavers all take part in the trade.

One named innovator is Chintakindi Mallesham, a Pochampally weaver. Wikipedia records that in 1999 he developed a machine to automate yarn winding, which the National Innovation Foundation recognised. Winding by hand had been a heavy task in the weaver household.
Our approach: name the weavers and dyers in every story, not only the cloth.
place: Bhoodan Pochampally is a census town in Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, about 40 to 50 km from Hyderabad. It had a population of 12,972 in 2011.

The village is also known as the birthplace of the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement. In April 1951, the landowner V. Ramachandra Reddy gave 100 acres after Vinoba Bhave asked for land for the landless. The village took the prefix Bhoodan from this.

In 2021 Pochampally was shortlisted by India's Ministry of Tourism and was recognised as one of the UNWTO Best Tourism Villages. A 2025 state tourism policy names it a priority destination, according to Wikipedia.

history.what: Telangana is counted as one of India's older ikat centres, along with Gujarat and Odisha. Written sources I read give no firm date for when weaving began at Pochampally.
Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan movement begins at the village in April; it later takes the name Bhoodan Pochampally.
Weaver Chintakindi Mallesham develops a yarn-winding machine, later recognised by the National Innovation Foundation.
Pochampally Ikat is registered as a Geographical Indication. Sources differ on the year: Wikipedia pages give both.
An Indian postage stamp of Rs 5 on Pochampally is reported by Wikipedia.
Pochampally is named among the UNWTO Best Tourism Villages.

future: Training: pair young people with master dyers and tie-makers so the slowest steps are not lost.
Livelihood: fair prices and direct sales, with clear labelling of handloom against powerloom copies.
Materials: safe dye handling and clean wastewater at the dyeing stage.
Documentation: record the design names and pattern sheets with the weavers who hold them.
Protection: use the GI tag actively and keep the register of authorised weavers up to date.

name: Puanchei Weaving
tagline: The most colourful Mizo puan, worn for dance and for weddings.
facts: Form: woven wrap-around cloth worn by women
Loom: traditional loin loom
Registered as Mizo Puanchei, Geographical Indication, August 2019
Applicant: Mizoram Art and Cultural Society (per IP Press)
art: Outlook Traveller calls Puanchei the most colourful of the Mizo puan. It is wrapped round the waist to cover the lower body and is worn at festive ceremonies and traditional dances. It is also part of a Mizo woman's trousseau.

Sources differ on how it is built. Outlook Traveller says a puan is usually two woven pieces sewn together but Puanchei is woven in three pieces, with the middle one narrowest. Another GI summary says two pieces are stitched together. The difference is not settled here.

A GI summary I could read through search says designs and motifs are put in by hand with supplementary yarns while weaving, and the cloth is woven on a traditional loin loom. I could not open the GI document itself.
Other Mizo weaves named by Outlook Traveller include Hmaram, Tawlhlohpuan, Ngotekherh and Pawndum. Pawndum is worn by men in the Khuallam dance.
artist: Puanchei is woven mostly by Mizo women. Outlook Traveller says Thenzawl in Serchhip district, about 43 km from Aizawl, is called the Handloom City. It does not link Thenzawl directly to Puanchei, though GI summaries name Aizawl and Thenzawl as production centres.
I found no named master weavers in the sources I could read.
place: Aizawl is the capital of Mizoram. Thenzawl is a town in Serchhip district known for handloom.
Puanchei is part of everyday and festival dress. Amar Chitra Katha describes it as part of the dress for the Cheraw dance.

history.what: Search results quoting a former Art and Culture director's book say Puanchei evolved from an older cloth called Puanlaisen, renamed around 1945. I could not read the book.
Mizo Puanchei received a Geographical Indication tag, along with Tawlhlohpuan, per IP Press and Outlook Traveller.
Puanchei remains a wedding cloth and a dance dress.

future: Training: weaving classes in Thenzawl and Aizawl for young women and men.
Livelihood: use the GI mark so that buyers can tell registered cloth from copies.
Materials: secure good yarn and natural or fast dyes.
Documentation: record old patterns and the Puanlaisen link with weavers.
Protection: GI enforcement and honest labelling of machine copies.

name: Reang (Risa) Weaving
tagline: Handwoven cloth of the Reang women, worn as a shawl, a chest cloth and a gift of honour.
facts: Makers: Reang (Bru) women, among other Tripuri communities
Loom: loin loom
Risa received a GI tag, announced in March 2024
Uses: upper garment, stole, headgear
art: Risa is a handwoven cloth of the tribal communities of Tripura. It is used as an upper garment, a stole, a shawl or a head covering. Women weave it on a loin loom, according to Wikipedia. Tripura Rural Livelihood Mission describes the weave as plain weave, one thread up and one down, with patterns built up by the weaver.

Among the Reang, Wikipedia names three pieces of women's dress: a long wraparound cloth (rnai), the risa that covers the chest, and the rikatouh that covers the upper body. Reang women usually weave their own colourful fabrics.

A fashion trade feature says Reang risa is marked by reds, deep blacks and geometric patterns, and that patterns, colours and methods differ from tribe to tribe. I treat this as a general account only.
Wikipedia notes a ceremony, Risa Sormani, in which an adolescent girl receives her first risa.
artist: Women are the weavers. The GI work was supported by NABARD and by the Tripura Rural Livelihood Mission, which promotes the cloth through its online marketplace. The Week names the Killa Mahila Cluster in Gomati district as one of the groups praised by the Chief Minister.
I did not find a source naming individual Reang weavers, so none are named.
place: The Reang, also called Bru, live mainly in Tripura, with smaller groups in Assam and Mizoram. The 2011 census figure cited by Wikipedia is 188,220 in Tripura, where they are the second most populous tribe.

Many Bru were displaced from Mizoram in 1997 and lived as refugees in Tripura. A 2020 agreement aimed to settle about 34,000 of them permanently in Tripura. Any weaving programme with these families depends on their settled homes and land.

history.what: I found no reliable source for when Reang weaving began.
Ethnic violence in Mizoram displaces tens of thousands of Bru into Tripura and Assam.
Wikipedia says the Chief Minister promoted risa after taking office.
A quadripartite agreement aims to settle displaced Bru permanently in Tripura.
Chief Minister Manik Saha announces that Risa has received a GI tag.

future: Training: pair young women with elder weavers, and teach pattern drafting.
Livelihood: use the GI tag and online marketplace so weavers receive the sale price.
Materials: reliable supply of cotton and colour-fast yarn.
Documentation: record Reang pattern names, which may differ from other Tripuri groups.
Protection: make clear which pieces are Reang work, as the GI covers Risa as a whole.

name: Sambalpuri Ikat
tagline: Threads tied and dyed before they are woven, so the pattern waits inside the yarn.
facts: Local name: bandha kala, the art of tying
Odisha work is mainly single ikat; double ikat is also woven
Main weaving communities: Bhuliya, Kostha and other Meher groups
Motifs: sankha (conch), chakra (wheel), phula (flower)
art: Ikat is a resist-dye method. The yarn is tied and dyed in the planned pattern before weaving, so the design is already on the threads when the loom is set. In Odisha this is called bandha, meaning tie, and the craft is often just called bandha kala.

Sahapedia describes Odisha's work as mostly single ikat, where either the warp or the weft is dyed. Its style is curvy, with soft, feathery outlines. Sahapedia contrasts this with the geometric Gujarat patola. Another Sahapedia account of the weaving process describes warp ikat, weft ikat and double ikat, where both are dyed, as the costliest and slowest.

The work is split into stages. A designer draws separate patterns for the border, the end piece (anchal) and the body. A tier counts and ties the knots with thin cotton thread, and bands cut from old tyres are also used to protect parts of the yarn from dye. A dyer then colours the yarn, in turn, from light to dark. Traditional dyes include turmeric, bark and seeds, and chemical dyes are also used today. Finally the weaver works at the handloom.

The motifs carry meaning. The conch (sankha), the wheel (chakra) and flowers (phula) are the best known. Animals, fish, the tortoise, serpent and peacock also appear. Named designs include Bichitrapuri, Pasapalli and Nagabandi. A cloth woven with Gita Govinda verses is used in the Jagannath temple, and its colours are said to match those of the Ratha Yatra chariots.
artist: The weavers are mostly from hereditary communities. Sahapedia names the Bhuliya, known for fine cotton, the Kostha, who work silk and tussar, and the Patras and Mehers of Nuapatna, Cuttack, Sonepur and Bargarh. A saree is rarely the work of one person. The family ties, dyes and weaves together, and one saree can take about four to eight days with household help, and much longer for fine work.
Master weavers often design the patterns, supply the yarn and buy back the cloth. Many weavers earn little, even those who have won awards.

Sahapedia names Padma Shri Kunjabihari Meher, who drew international attention to the craft in the 1970s through demonstrations, and his son Surendra Meher, who won a National Award in 1991. It also names Padma Shri Krutartha Acharya, who founded a cooperative that improved weavers' pay, and the poet Gangadhar Meher, from the weaver community, whose verses inspired designs.
place: Sambalpuri cloth takes its name from the Sambalpur region, but Sahapedia stresses that most production is in Bargarh district, with over 12,000 looms. Barpali in Balangir is another well-known centre. Sonepur, Cuttack's Nuapatna and Badamba, and parts of Balasore and Mayurbhanj also weave ikat.
State bodies such as Boyanika, Utkalika and Sambalpuri Bastralaya were set up after Independence to support and sell Odisha's textiles.

history.when: Traditionally dated to about the 13th century
history.what: Sahapedia cites R.N. Mehta, who suggests Odisha's ikat may go back to about the 13th century CE, and says possible traces appear in temple sculpture at Konark, Saintala and Sonepur.
Oral history says Bhuliya weavers migrated from Madhya Pradesh and brought Gujarat patola know-how. Sources differ on the date and route.
Sahapedia lists the Maratha period, colonial trade, the Charter Act of 1833, the famine of 1865-66 and chemical dyes among the causes of decline.
State agencies and cooperatives were set up to support weavers and marketing.
Wider recognition begins, with demonstrations and sales across India and abroad.
Demand falls as cheap printed and machine-woven copies spread.

future: Fair pay: support weaver cooperatives so that a share of the price reaches the people who tie, dye and weave.
Training: keep the tier's and dyer's skills alive, not only the weaver's, with younger family members and apprentices.
Materials: stable thread prices and access to credit, since many small weavers borrow yarn at interest.
Documentation: record the named designs and their meanings with the weaver families.
Protection: label genuine handwoven cloth clearly so buyers can tell it from power-loom copies.

name: Sikkimese Carpets
tagline: Hand-knotted wool carpets, woven upright by Bhutia women with Buddhist motifs.
facts: Hand-knotted on fixed vertical looms
Made mainly by Bhutia women
Motifs: mythical birds, lotuses, snow lions, eight lucky signs
Source evidence for this entry is limited
art: Young INTACH's craft map says Sikkimese carpets are hand-knotted and woven on fixed vertical looms that stand upright against a wall. The patterns are Tibetan in style and include mythical birds, lotus flowers, snow lions and the eight Buddhist lucky signs.
We could not open a detailed source on wool, dyes or the knotting process, so this entry does not describe them.
artist: The same source names Bhutia women as the main makers. It separates this craft from Lepcha weaving and from blanket weaving, which it says is done by Nepalese women from sheep wool.
We did not find a source we could read that names individual weavers or workshops.
place: The carpets are made across Sikkim. Young INTACH lists the carpet craft with Bhutia women of Sikkim, alongside Lepcha weaving, blanket weaving and mask making.

history.what: We could not verify the early history. Some web pages call it one of the oldest carpet traditions in the world, which we did not confirm from a reliable source.
The carpet remains a handmade, upright-loom craft with Buddhist and Tibetan motifs.

future: Training: apprenticeships so younger women learn knotting and design.
Livelihood: fair prices and a clear label of origin for handmade pieces.
Materials: dependable supply of good wool and dyes.
Documentation: write down the motifs and workshops, as the research for this entry found little.
Protection: consider a GI or craft-mark for authentic Sikkim carpets.

name: Sozni Embroidery
tagline: A needle-and-thread art that looks the same on both sides of a shawl.
facts: Local names: Sozankari, Sozan Kaari
Name from Persian sozan, needle
Dorukha: the pattern is identical on both sides
Usual base: pashmina, in silk or wool thread
art: Sozni is fine hand embroidery from Kashmir. It is worked with silk or woollen thread, most often on pashmina. Its name comes from sozan, the word for needle.

Its best-known feature is called dorukha. The stitches look the same on both sides of the cloth, with no loose thread and no visible knot. The main stitch is satin stitch. Other stitches, such as chain and herringbone, are also used.

The motifs are drawn from the Valley: the chinar leaf, the almond (badam), paisley, cypress trees, flowers and vines, and sometimes birds such as parrots and kingfishers or hunting scenes (shikargah). Pernia's encyclopedia lists four ways of laying out the work: jamawar, which covers almost all the cloth; jaaldar, a lighter spread of stitches; butidaar, with small motifs; and palladar, with embroidery only on the borders.

A designer called a naqash sketches the pattern and often cuts it into a wooden block, which is used to print the outline on the cloth. The sozankar, the embroiderer, then stitches it by hand. Time taken depends on the work. The pages we read give anything from a few months to over a year.
artist: The two roles, naqash and sozankar, work together. One page says each shawl is embroidered by one craftsman and that a piece begun by one hand is not finished by another. We could not confirm this from a second source, so treat it as a common saying of the trade.

The craft is taught by practice. Pernia's encyclopedia says that just learning the grip and movement of the needle can take up to six months. Women in rural Kashmir often take part, sometimes in small groups, says a craft article we read.
We did not find reliable, named master embroiderers in the sources we could open, so we do not name any here.
place: Sozni belongs to the Kashmir Valley, and Srinagar is its main market. Pashmina, the usual base cloth, is also a Kashmiri specialty.

The Valley's gardens and trees are on the cloth. Chinar, almond blossom, cypress and kingfisher all grow or fly there, and the embroiderers bring them to the shawl. Today the stitchwork also appears on kaftans, kurtas and cardigans.

history.what: Pernia's encyclopedia links the craft to the Persian Sufi Mir Syed Ali Hamdani, who is said to have come to Kashmir with about 700 companions, some of them sozni craftsmen. This is a traditional account, and other sources give other dates.
Craft writers say sozni flourished under Mughal patronage. Pernia says it was used on jamawar, the long shawls worn by Mughal emperors.
Embroidered shawls reached European markets, according to an Exotic India article.
The same article says industrial mass production cut demand.
Government bodies, heritage groups and collectors helped revive the craft, the article says.

future: Training: formal apprenticeships with fair pay, since mastery of the needle alone takes months.
Livelihood: pay embroiderers fairly for the months a single piece takes, and name them on the finished work.
Materials: protect real pashmina from blends and imitations sold under the same name.
Documentation: record designs, stitches and the vocabulary of naqash and sozankar, and the names of living masters.
Protection: check official records for GI status. We saw GI claims in search results but could not confirm them from a page we read.

name: Sualkuchi Muga Silk
tagline: Golden silk from Assam's own silkworm, woven on the Brahmaputra's bank.
facts: Medium: Muga, Pat and Eri silk
Technique: handloom weaving
Garments: mekhela chador
art: Assam produces three native silks: muga, pat and eri. Muga is the most celebrated: a natural golden-yellow silk, found only in Assam, which grows richer with washing and use.
Weavers make the mekhela chador, Assam's two-piece traditional dress, with motifs such as flowers, birds and the kingkhap (a rich brocade pattern).
artist: Weaving is largely done by women, often at home looms. Many households in Sualkuchi keep a loom, and girls grow up learning to weave.
Today's weavers also experiment with new designs and colours, while the old patterns are being documented.
Our approach: profile weavers by name and share the full journey from cocoon to cloth.
place: Sualkuchi, on the north bank of the Brahmaputra, near Guwahati, is often called the 'Manchester of the East' for its concentration of looms.
The Brahmaputra floods shape village life, and Assam's wet climate suits the silk-producing host trees.

history.what: Silk-making in Assam is recorded for many centuries and is closely tied to the Kamarupa and Ahom kingdoms.
Royal patronage supported the silk and textile industries.
Power looms and imitation silks challenged handloom weavers.
Muga silk has a geographical indication, and Sualkuchi is a centre for both tradition and tourism.

future: Certify real muga so buyers can trust what they buy.
Support rearers of silkworms, whose income is often forgotten.
Flood-proof looms and stock for weaving families.

name: Sujni Embroidery
tagline: Running stitch on old cloth, once for newborn quilts and now for women's own stories.
facts: Place: villages around Bhusura, Muzaffarpur
Stitch: fine running stitch, with chain stitch for outlines
Made only by women
GI registered 21 September 2006, per Wikipedia
art: Sujni is a quilting and embroidery tradition from Muzaffarpur district. Wikipedia says it began as quilts for newborns, made from layers of old saris and dhotis held with running stitch. The name is explained as su (easy) and jani (birth).

The main stitch is a fine running stitch in thread that matches the cloth. Outlines are often chain stitch in black, brown or red. The GI record describes the stitch as visible on both sides of the cloth. Makers now use cotton, tussar silk and other fabrics.

Early motifs included the sun, clouds, fertility signs and protective animals. Wikipedia says thread colours also carried meaning. Newer pieces often show the lives of women: dowry, domestic abuse, education and women's rights. A quilt may show hardship on one side and women earning or speaking in public on the other.
artist: Sujni is made by women, in their homes. Wikipedia counts about 600 women in 22 villages, while other sources say about 15 villages. The figures differ between sources.

The craft had nearly died out. Sources agree on a revival in 1988 in Bhusura. Wikipedia credits Nirmal Devi of the Mahila Vikas Sahyog Samiti. Another account credits the non-profit ADITHI and Viji Srinivasan working with village women, with Nirmala Devi among the first to join.
For many women the work was the first income they controlled.
place: Bhusura is in the Ghaighatti block of Muzaffarpur district, north Bihar. The GI record says the work is done mainly in about 15 villages around it, and in some pockets of Madhubani.
This is a flat, flood-prone region of the Ganga plain. Households here have long reused cloth, and quilting from old textiles is part of that habit.

history.what: Wikipedia says the earliest known tradition of sujni quilts dates to this century.
Quilts were made for newborns and as household items.
Revival in Bhusura. Wikipedia credits Nirmal Devi and the Mahila Vikas Sahyog Samiti. Another account credits ADITHI and Viji Srinivasan.
GI registered as Sujani Embroidery Work of Bihar, application number 74 (Wikipedia gives this date; we could not open the registry entry itself).

future: Training: pass the stitch to girls, and train makers in newer fabrics and products
Livelihood: fair, regular orders so women are paid for their hours
Materials: reuse old cloth where possible, which is how the art began
Documentation: record the oldest motifs and the colour meanings with older makers
Protection: use the GI to prevent machine copies and to name makers on pieces

name: Sungudi
tagline: Cloth tied knot by knot until white circles bloom on the dye.
facts: Tie-dye textile of Madurai
Tiny thread knots resist the dye
Brought by Saurashtra weavers
Madurai Sungudi has GI status (2005)
art: Sungudi is a tie-dyed cloth. Selvedge describes how the artisan pinches the cloth with the fingertips and ties tiny thread knots at points marked in a pattern. After dyeing, the threads are taken off and white circles are left on the coloured ground.

Selvedge says the name comes from Sanskrit and Saurashtra words roughly meaning zero and tie, referring to the circles. Two-colour designs need the tying and dyeing to be repeated and can take about fifty days.
Saris are traditionally hand-woven cotton, and silk versions are now made too. The artisan ties the design in the unwoven body between the border and end panels.
Motifs named in the article include the star pattern, leheriya diagonal lines made of dots, grid designs, the V-shaped vanki, and kolam, inspired by floor patterns of rice flour.
artist: Sungudi is passed down in families. Selvedge profiles Ramesh and Vasumathi, who learned knotting from relatives and have taught their family, friends and more than 2,000 design students and enthusiasts.

The article says about fifty community members now practise the art. One sari takes roughly 20 to 30 days. Natural dyes from leaves, flowers, fruits and roots are used at home, while some cloth is dyed with synthetic dyes at a unit nearby.
place: The craft belongs to Madurai, the old temple city on the Vaigai river in southern Tamil Nadu.
It is linked to the Saurashtrian community, who came from Saurashtra in Gujarat and settled in the south.

history.what: Selvedge says weavers from Saurashtra settled in South India under the Vijayanagar Empire.

Selvedge says King Thirumalai Nayakar invited their descendants to weave in Madurai. They brought a tie-dye method from Saurashtra and made it a local style. Other sources place the migration at different times.
Madurai Sungudi received a Geographical Indication tag, according to Selvedge.
The article says fewer than ten people were then practising the craft.
Interest in natural-dyed saris is said to be growing again.

future: Train young people in knotting, since it is a slow, learned skill.
Keep natural dye work alive and pay for its extra time.
Use the GI mark so buyers can tell hand-tied cloth from printed copies.
Document motifs and the names of tying families.
Link artisans directly to buyers and design schools for stable orders.

name: Tussar Silk of Jharkhand
tagline: Wild silk with a golden sheen, from forest cocoons to handloom.
facts: Fibre: wild tussar silk
Cocoons mostly tended by tribal communities
Jharkhand is described as a leading producer
Ghicha is a handwoven tussar variety
art: Tussar, also spelled tasar, is a wild silk. Wikipedia says it comes from Antheraea silkworms that feed on trees such as asan (Terminalia) and sal. The silk is coarse, with a dull gold sheen and a rich texture.

To get the silk, cocoons are softened by boiling. Madras Courier describes a process for ghicha silk: cocoons are soaked in a mix of sugar, water and soda and boiled, women unravel the thread by hand, and it is dried, wound and spun into yarn. Male weavers then weave it on handlooms. The report says the cloth is finished in Bihar.
The saree is the main product, though tussar also goes into furnishing fabrics, handicrafts and stitched clothes.
artist: Wikipedia says the cocoons are largely tended by tribal communities, and many are collected from forests.

Madras Courier says women do the central but often unseen work of reeling and spinning, while men weave. It reports that weavers earn about Rs 550 a saree, many face debt, and cheaper imitations compete with handwoven cloth. Prices of sarees are given as Rs 3,000 to 7,000. These are one report's figures.
We could not find a reliable source naming individual weavers or rearing families, so none are named here.
place: Madras Courier names Bhagaiya, near Godda in the Santhal Pargana, as a weaving centre, and says dry cocoons are bought at Jagdalpur in Chhattisgarh. Forest-based rearing is also pinned at Kharsawan in West Singhbhum, but we did not open a source for it, so that pin is approximate.
Wikipedia says Jharkhand has recently emerged as the largest producer of tussar in India. Other major centres are Bhagalpur in Bihar and Malda in West Bengal.

history.what: Wikipedia notes that tribal communities tend and collect the cocoons. We did not find a dated origin.
One source says that cocoons from Jharkhand were mostly sold to weaving centres in other states. This comes from a secondary report.
Jharkhand was formed as a state.
Wikipedia describes the state as having recently become the largest producer.

future: Train rearing families in spinning and weaving so more of the value stays in Jharkhand.
Give women reelers and spinners recognised skills training and fair pay.
Protect the sal and asan forests where the worms feed, and give tribal rearers secure access.
Label handwoven ghicha and tussar clearly so buyers can tell it from machine copies.
Document the rearing calendar and local knowledge of the families in an open archive.

name: Uppada Jamdani
tagline: Light, near-sheer handloom saris with patterns woven into the cloth, two weavers to a loom.
facts: Technique: jamdani, motifs woven in as the cloth is made
Loom: handloom, two weavers per loom
About two months for one sari (one source)
Holds a Geographical Indication
art: Uppada Jamdani saris are handwoven in Uppada, a coastal village in Andhra Pradesh. In jamdani the design is woven into the cloth, not printed or stitched on afterwards. Zari is used in the patterns.

Utsavpedia says two weavers work on each loom and a sari can take about two months. The cloth is light and almost translucent. The same page says the warp is usually cotton and also refers to silk varieties, so descriptions of the fibre differ.
Utsavpedia says the designs are closely identified with Andhra Pradesh. It does not list the motifs, and I could not verify specific motif names.
artist: Utsavpedia names the Padmasali community as the weavers of Uppada saris. Wikipedia instead says the Devangs, skilled handloom weavers, have lived near Uppada in large numbers since ancient times. I could not settle this, so both are given.
Weaving families today source designs and yarn and weave at home. Utsavpedia says it took the weavers considerable time to learn the hand skills when the technique was introduced.
Utsavpedia credits the textile designer Ghanshyam Sarode with introducing Uppada Silk, and calls him a revivalist of Indian ethnic fashion.
place: Uppada lies on the west coast of the Bay of Bengal, about 45 km from Tuni, in Kothapalli mandal of Kakinada district. Earlier it was counted in East Godavari. Wikipedia also calls it a fishing village known for prawns.
The jamdani craft there sits beside a fishing economy, which means weavers share the village with another demanding trade.

history.what: Jamdani is a technique with roots in Bengal. According to Utsavpedia it declined in the 19th century and revived slowly in the 20th.
Utsavpedia says the jamdani technique was introduced in Uppada in this year, with designs drawn from Andhra Pradesh.
Utsavpedia says the range took about ten years to gain recognition and popularity.
Wikipedia says Uppada Jamdani holds a GI for Andhra Pradesh. I did not find the registration year in a source I read.

future: Pay weavers fair wages for a month or two of work per sari, and show the hours on the label.
Set up training so that more young weavers can learn jamdani technique from the senior ones.
Document traditional and new Uppada designs on graph paper, as weavers' own record.
Source fine yarn and zari at fair prices for home weavers.
Use the GI mark so buyers can tell a hand-woven Uppada sari from a power-loom copy.

name: Zardozi
tagline: Embroidery in gold-wrapped thread, once for royal tents and now for wedding wear.
facts: Name: Persian, zar (gold) and dozi (sewing)
Frame: the fabric is stretched on a wooden adda
Lucknow zardozi: GI registered in 2013
GI area: Lucknow and six nearby districts
art: Zardozi is heavy metal embroidery. The name comes from Persian words meaning gold and sewing. Metal wire wrapped around silk thread is stitched onto cloth, usually in floral patterns. Wikipedia lists the many metal elements used, such as flattened wire (badla), coiled wire (salma, dabka), flat metallic thread (tilla), and sequins (sitara).

Outlook Traveller describes the Lucknow method. The fabric is stretched tight on a wooden frame called an adda. The design is drawn on tracing paper, pricked with a needle, and transferred to the cloth with a swab of kerosene and dye. The embroidery then follows the outline. Lucknow work uses a cotton filling called bukram under the metal to raise the pattern and give it depth.

Early work used real silver wire and gold leaf. Today many workers use copper wire with a gold or silver finish, and plastic or glass stones in place of semi-precious ones. Outlook Traveller notes that cheaper materials have made zardozi affordable to more buyers.
The same article contrasts the regional styles. Lucknow work is described as ornate and spread out, while Hyderabad and Agra work is described as more minimal.
artist: Zardozi is done by hand, often in family workshops where several generations work together. Outlook Traveller says the work is demanding: it involves sharp wires, close focus and speed. The article does not name individual artisans, and neither do the other pages I read, so none are named here.

The GI registration lets artisans, distributors and retailers in Lucknow and the six districts around it use the 'Lucknow Zardozi' name and its authenticity mark. The GI Registry announcement is dated August 2013.
Zardozi is now used well beyond clothing. Outlook Traveller reports that blended fabrics and modular machines have extended it to purses, belts, shawls and shoes.
place: Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh, is the best-known centre. Wikipedia names the GI districts as Barabanki, Unnao, Sitapur, Rae Bareli, Hardoi and Amethi. It also lists Agra, Bareilly and Farrukhabad as smaller centres in the state, and Hyderabad, Bhopal and Delhi elsewhere in India.
Zardozi is not only Indian. Wikipedia places it in Iran, Central Asia, Pakistan and India, so Lucknow's claim is to a particular style and to the GI, not to the craft as a whole.
The Outlook Traveller article says the GI helps tell Lucknow work apart from work made in Delhi, Bhopal, Hyderabad, Agra and Kashmir.

history.what: The craft is Persian in name and is found across Iran, Central Asia and the subcontinent. One news site says zardozi existed from the Rig Veda. I could not find support for that, so treat it as a claim.

Outlook Traveller says the Mughals brought zardozi from Persia. Wikipedia says it flourished in the 17th century and was favoured by the elite, used on royal tents, wall hangings and the trappings of elephants and horses.
Sources attribute the decline to loss of royal patronage and industrialisation. One article ties it to Aurangzeb's rule; sources differ on timing.
Outlook Traveller says the craft flourished under the Nawabs of Lucknow.
Wikipedia says interest revived after Independence, and zardozi is now one of the most popular embroideries on the subcontinent.
Outlook Traveller says a trend in the 1990s made Lucknow zardozi dominant in couture and ceremonial wear.
The GI Registry grants Geographical Indication registration to Lucknow zardozi.

future: Training: pay apprentices a living wage, since the work is slow and hard on eyes and hands.
Livelihood: link family workshops to buyers who pay for hand work, not machine copies, and use the GI mark to show the difference.
Materials: be honest about what is in the thread, real zari or coated copper, so buyers know what they are paying for.
Documentation: record stitches, terms such as badla, salma and dabka, and the pricking-and-pouncing method with the families who use them.
Protection: use the GI against imitations from other regions or from machines.
